bio.en: Jason Droege is the CEO of Scale AI—his first interview since succeeding founder Alexandr Wang after the Meta deal—and previously co-founded Uber Eats, which grew into a multi-billion-dollar business that helped save Uber during the pandemic.
bio.zh: Jason Droege 是 Scale AI 的 CEO——这是他接替创始人 Alexandr Wang（赴 Meta 后）后的首次采访，他此前联合创办了 Uber Eats，将其发展为价值数十亿美元的业务，并在疫情期间拯救了 Uber。

summary.en: Jason explains why enterprise AI takes 6–12 months to become robust enough to automate real processes, and why the trend is shifting from models that 'know things' to models that 'do things' via agents. He describes Scale's pioneering role in data labeling, training data, and evals—work that increasingly requires PhDs and professionals doing tasks that take hours—and how that is what actually makes frontier models smarter. The conversation also covers the high bar he sets for new businesses and what unique insight justifies starting one.
summary.zh: Jason 解释了为何企业级 AI 需要 6–12 个月才能足够稳健到自动化真实流程，以及为何趋势正从“知道事情”的模型转向通过智能体“做事”的模型。他描述了 Scale 在数据标注、训练数据和 evals 领域的开创性角色——这类工作越来越需要博士和专业人士完成耗时数小时的任务，而这正是前沿模型变聪明的真正来源。对话还涵盖他对新业务设定的高门槛，以及何种独特洞见才值得去创业。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's been a lot of talk these days about AI not delivering on the promise that we hear, especially at enterprises.
turns.zh: 最近有很多关于人工智能未能兑现我们所期望的承诺的讨论，尤其是在企业领域。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: These things take 6 to 12 months to get them truly robust enough where an important process can be automated. Like with any of these major tech revolutions, headlines tell one story and then on the ground, laying broadband means you need to dig up every single road in America to lay it. Someone's got to dig up the road or someone's got to run the undersea cable.
turns.zh: 这些事情需要6到12个月的时间才能真正变得足够强大，从而实现重要流程的自动化。就像任何重大技术革命一样，头条新闻讲述了一个故事，但现实情况是，铺设宽带意味着你需要挖开美国每条道路来进行铺设。总得有人去挖路，或者有人去铺设海底光缆。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything you think people don't truly grasp or understand about where AI models are going to be in the next two, three years?

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: The general trend right now is going from models knowing things to models doing things. The next question becomes, what can it do for me? How does the agent make decisions for you?
turns.zh: 当前的总体趋势是从模型"知晓事物"转向模型"执行任务"。接下来的问题是，它能为我做些什么？智能体如何为你做出决策？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's talk about Scale and this whole world of AI that you're in, you essentially pioneered data labeling, trading data, creating evals for labs.
turns.zh: 让我们谈谈Scale以及你所处的整个AI领域。你基本上开创了数据标注、数据交易、为实验室创建评估等领域。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: 18 months ago, you would get a short story and it would say, "Is this short story better than this short story?" And now you're at a point where one task is building an entire website by one of the world's best web developers, or it is explaining some very nuanced topic on cancer to a model. These tasks now take hours of time and they require PhDs and professionals.
turns.zh: 18个月前，你会得到一个简短的故事，问"这个故事比那个故事更好吗？"而现在你已经到了这样一个阶段：一项任务需要世界上最优秀的网页开发者来构建整个网站，或者向模型解释一些关于癌症的非常复杂的主题。这些任务现在需要数小时的时间，还需要博士和专业人士才能完成。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've talked to a bunch of people that have worked with you over the years, and I heard a lot about just how high of a bar you set for new businesses.
turns.zh: 我与多年来与你合作过的人进行了交谈，他们经常提到你为新企业设定的标准非常高。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: From an entrepreneurship standpoint, it truly is about what insight do I have? Why am I so lucky to have this insight? turns.zh: 从创业的角度来看，这真正关乎我有什么样的洞察力？为什么我如此幸运能拥有这种洞察力？在一百万个创业者都在思考、聪明且尝试各种方法的世界里，为什么我可能处于一个可能拥有其他人没有的洞察力的位置？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As I was researching your background and prepping for this podcast, I learned a really interesting fun fact about you that I don't think a lot of people know. So Travis Kalanick, he had a startup before Uber. It was called Scour. It was a peer-to-peer file sharing app, and then I think got shut down. You were his co-founder. What's just a lesson that has stuck with you from that experience that you've taken with you to future places you've worked and built product at?
turns.zh: 在研究你的背景并为这次播客做准备时，我发现了一个关于你的有趣趣闻，我觉得很多人都不知道。特拉维斯·卡兰尼克在创立优步之前曾有一家创业公司，叫Scour。这是一款P2P文件共享应用，但后来被关闭了。你当时是他的联合创始人。这是你职业生涯的早期阶段。我猜我们可以聊聊这段经历中的诸多故事。那么让我先问你一个问题：从这段经历中，你有什么收获，至今仍对后续的工作和产品开发有所启发？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: I mean, there's so many lessons. I like to pick one. I think that the main lesson is that in business and in startups, everything's negotiable. I think that's the main thing. Because we were 19 at the time, 19, 20 at the time, we built this search engine in a dorm room and we were running it out of the dorm room and our first URL was scour.cs.ucla.edu. These things were not necessarily in fractions at the time, but we were just being practical. It was basically a project that we had started, and so we built the search engine and people started using it and we thought we would get in trouble, but it turned out the computer science department was excited about it even though we had basically parked a domain on their servers and we were using our own computers in the dorms to serve up this website and product. (00:07:46): And then, when we got into financing, the financing process was fascinating, and this is where the everything is negotiable lesson came from, which is, it was Ron Burkle and Mike Ovitz, who are the initial investors in the business. We were in LA, so we were at UCLA, so we were not quite wired into the entire Sand Hill Road scene. And as we were doing the deal, the terms kept changing on us. We thought you went and raised money and it was like, "Oh, we'll get a few million dollars at a $5 million valuation." This is back when that was actually a series A valuation. And then over the course of the deal, it was like, "We're doing the deal. We're not doing the deal. Oh, you should give us 50% of the company. Oh, you should give us 75% of the company. Oh, if you want to sign the document today, this person's going to show up for breakfast and if you don't sign today and give us 80% of the company, the person's not going to show up." (00:08:38): It was just completely wild, the things that we saw from day one of what can happen in business, and we thought there was a way to do things, and at a very young age we realized there is no way to do things. There is just the way that you can negotiate your way through the world, which I actually think influenced Travis heavily and then me later heavily at Uber in terms of if you can imagine it and it makes sense and you can align incentives, then it can happen. But there is no way. And to learn that at 19 or 20 years old I think was highly imprinting.
turns.zh:
其实有很多经验教训。我想挑一个最重要的——在商业和创业领域，一切都是可以协商的。当时我们19岁，19、20岁，在宿舍里开发了一个搜索引擎，放在宿舍服务器上运行，首个网址是scour.cs.ucla.edu。当时这些东西没有精确的衡量标准，我们只是务实行事。项目启动后，人们开始使用它，我们以为会惹上麻烦，但计算机科学系的人对此很兴奋，尽管我们把域名放在了他们的服务器上，在宿舍用自己的电脑提供服务。
(00:07:46)：接下来是融资环节，整个过程很有意思。这里就体现了"一切皆可协商"的道理。最初的投资人是罗恩·伯克尔和迈克·奥维茨。我们在洛杉矶，离UCLA很近，当时对整个硅谷风投圈不太熟悉。融资过程中，条款不断变更。我们以为融资成功，结果对方说："估值5000万美元，拿几百万美元。"这在当时可是A轮融资标准。然后又改口："不融资了。要你公司50%股份。75%吧。今天签合同，人会来吃早餐；不签，80%股份也没人来了。"
(00:08:38)：从第一天起，我们就见识到商业世界的无常。我们以为有固定套路，但实际没有。只学会了如何通过谈判达成目的。这对特拉维斯影响很大，我后来在优步也深有体会——只要能设想出可行方案，协调好利益，就能成事。但根本没有标准答案。19、20岁就领悟到这一点，让我刻骨铭心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is an amazing lesson. What happened to Scour? It got shut down, I think. What happened there?
turns.zh: 真是深刻的教训。Scour后来怎么了？好像被关停了。具体情况如何？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Well, yeah, so basically what Scour was was it was a multimedia search engine and then peer-to-peer file sharing network. But what it was used for was finding free content. And at the time, the laws were on this were pretty ambiguous because we weren't, mix tapes were legal, but this was like a hyperversion of that. But we were eventually sued for a quarter of a trillion dollars. So I guess if you're going to experience something that's potentially as life devastating as that, doing it when you're, I think we were 21 or 22 at the time is the time to do it, but it was just this very cold splash of water about how the real world really works, because the MBAA and the RAA were the ones who sued us, the entertainment industry sued us or the associations that represent the entertainment industry, and then they settled it for $1 million. (00:10:08): So we're like, "Wait, you wanted a quarter of a trillion dollars and then you settle for $1 million." And of course they were just trying to drive us in a bankruptcy, drive us out of the market, and these are established companies. So we're like, "If these guys don't have a playbook to follow, they just make up numbers, then wow, how should we navigate the rest of our lives?"
turns.zh:
嗯，对，基本上Scour是一个多媒体搜索引擎和点对点文件共享网络。但它主要用于寻找免费内容。当时相关法律条款相当模糊，因为我们当时还是21、22岁，所以做这种事倒也无妨。但最终我们被起诉，要赔偿高达25万亿美元。当时如果经历这种可能毁掉一生的法律纠纷，在我看来，21、22岁正是该经历的时候，但这也让我们深刻认识到现实世界的残酷规则——因为起诉我们的是美国唱片业协会（RIAA）和美国音乐版权商协会（MPAA）等代表娱乐业的机构，最终我们以100万美元达成和解。

（00:10:08）：所以我们当时就问，“等等，你们之前要25万亿美元，现在却只赔偿100万美元？”当然，他们就是想让我们破产，退出市场，而这些都是大公司。所以我们想，如果这些家伙连规则都没有，随便乱定数字，那我们该如何度过余生？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's talk about Scale and this whole world of AI that you're in. This is the first interview that you're doing since taking over CEO at Scale. I'm honored to have you here to talk through this stuff. This is also the first interview you're doing since the whole Meta deal, which is very complicated, confused a lot of people. So I'm just curious to hear the current state of Scale, what people should know. For example, what's your relationship with Meta? What's your relationship with Alex? What is the current state of Scale?
turns.zh: 接下来聊聊Scale以及你所处的AI世界。这是你接任Scale CEO后的首次采访。很荣幸能邀请你来谈谈这些事。这也是你在Meta交易后的首次采访，整个交易非常复杂，让很多人困惑。所以我很好奇想了解Scale目前的状况，以及人们应该知道的信息。比如，你和Meta的关系如何？你和Alex的关系如何？Scale目前的状况如何？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Yeah, so Scale is a fully independent company. The transaction was Meta invested a little bit over $14 billion to get 49% of the company, non-voting stock, didn't take a new board seat. Alex fills the board seat. So the board is the same, the governance is largely the same. There's no preferential access to anything that Meta has. There's no preferential relationship. I mean, we've had a longstanding relationship with Meta on the data side of the business for a long time and even on some business development related things to maybe working on things in government together, et cetera. And so, those might get bigger just as we're closer now, but there's nothing that prevents us from doing things with other parties and they have no access to anything that they wouldn't have had otherwise. All the privacy still in place, all the data security still in place that was there before. (00:11:47): And in fact, only about 15 people went over in the transaction. So Scale has about 1,100 employees or so now, and we have two major businesses. Each of those businesses, each of them has hundreds of millions of revenue. So we have two unicorns inside the company today that sustains. The business has grown every month since the deal happened, which I've read, the reporting is not consistently reported. We haven't talked about it, so this is part of getting the word out and we're excited to continue to build, deliver data, and do what we did before.
turns.zh:
是的，Scale是一家完全独立的公司。交易是Meta投资略超140亿美元获得49%的非投票权股份，没有新董事席位。Alex填补了董事席位。所以董事会还是原班人马，治理模式基本不变。Meta没有任何优先访问权限，也没有特殊关系。我的意思是，我们和Meta在数据业务方面长期合作，甚至在一些商业开发相关事务上也有合作，比如共同参与政府项目等。随着我们的关系日益紧密，这些合作可能会进一步深化，但没有任何条款阻止我们与其他方合作，他们也无法获取原本无法获取的信息。所有隐私保护和数据安全措施都依然到位。

（00:11:47）：事实上，交易中只有约15人加入了新公司。所以Scale目前约有1100名员工，我们有两大业务板块。每个业务板块的营收都达数亿美元。如今公司内部有两家估值达数十亿美元的独角兽公司，业务自交易以来每月都在增长。不过相关报道并不一致，我们之前没有谈及此事，所以这次采访也是为了让更多人了解情况。我们很兴奋能继续前进，提供数据服务，延续之前的工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the company today, independent, its own company. Alex, just to be clear, he works at Meta now. He's no longer at Scale.
turns.zh: 所以现在的公司是独立的，属于自己的公司。Alex，说明一下，他现在在Meta工作，不再在Scale了。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Yeah, that's right. Excuse me, I should have talked about that more.
turns.zh: 是啊，没错。抱歉，我本该多讲讲这个的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that's really interesting. So basically, it was an investment. Some people left to join Meta, the company continues, you're running the ship. Let's talk about this whole space that you guys essentially pioneered, I don't know best way to call it, data labeling, training data, creating evals for labs. You guys were at this before anyone even knew this was a thing. I know even Scale pivoted into this market from other things. I think there was a bunch of stuff they tried with self-driving cars and all these things, and then it's like, "Oh shit, AI labs need this data." (00:12:57): One of the main stories I've been hearing is, and I've had a bunch of CEOs from this space on the podcast, is that there's been this big shift from the way, from what Scale had pioneered and had been doing for a long time, which is generalists, low-cost labor training. From that to now, labs mostly need experts, lawyers, doctors, engineers doing training, writing evals, things like that. I'm curious just what you're seeing, how that's impacting you guys, where you think things are heading, what people should know about this whole market of data training data.
turns.zh: 我觉得这真的很有趣。简单来说，这就是一项投资。有些人离开去加入Meta了，公司还在继续运作，而你现在掌管大局。咱们来聊聊你们开创的这个领域吧，我不知道该怎么准确称呼它——数据标注、训练数据、为实验室创建评估体系。在别人还没意识到这块市场存在之前，你们就已经在做这些了。我知道就连Scale也从其他领域转向了这个市场。他们之前尝试过自动驾驶汽车之类的项目，但后来发现：“天哪，AI实验室急需这些数据啊。”（00:12:57）我听过很多这个领域的CEO在播客上谈到的一个主要转变：从Scale长期倡导的通才型、低成本劳动力培训模式，转向如今实验室主要需要专家——律师、医生、工程师——来负责训练、编写评估报告之类的工作。我很好奇你们对此有何观察，这对你们有何影响，你们认为这个数据训练市场将何去何从，以及人们应该对整个数据训练市场有何了解。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Yeah, totally. I think the current positioning out there from competitors is just bogus. So I'll start with that and then maybe talk a little bit about, I'll explain what I mean by that in a second. But I think it's important to just give 30 seconds on what the history of Scale is and what's the thread going back to 2016. So Alex had this insight in very early days that the important thing to models was data. And I think he was 19 or 20 years old at the time as well. And so, he's like, "Okay, well what business would I create around this?" And the business that he created around it was, okay, let's do labeling for autonomous vehicles, because if you label the data that they have, the cars do better. And then, that wave turned into the computer vision wave, which we have a relationship with the Department of Defense where we do labeling for them, and that was in 2020. (00:14:21): And then, you move forward and the models have gotten better over this period of time. And so, as models get better, they need different types of data. So we've constantly been adapting to the type of data that models need to be successful. And so, then the gen AI wave hit, and this went through the moon or to the moon. And so, as part of that, that industry is changing constantly too. So it is correct that when the models came out two or three years ago, I mean we remember using them, they would hallucinate all the time, they would get basic answers wrong, they didn't know which poem was better, this poem or that poem. And that was the state of labeling a couple years ago. And things have changed quickly and we've changed with it. And now the state for everyone, and we've been at the forefront of all of this, is expert data labeling, more sophisticated tasks. (00:15:15): So to give you a sense of what the task was 18 months ago, I've been here about 13 months. So I was interviewing and I remember seeing it. You would get a short story and it would say, "Is this short story better than this short story?" And then you would edit it and be like, "Yeah, it would be better if it was this," and you would give some preference ranking to it. It was pretty basic 18 months ago, and you had the rise of some experts, but the models were so far behind that they needed just even the basic stuff they needed. And now, you're at a point where a task is, one task is building an entire website by one of the world's best web developers, or it is explaining some very nuanced topic on cancer to a model. And these tasks now take hours of time and they require PhDs and professionals. (00:16:01): So to give you a stat to back this up, 80% of the people that we have on our expert network have a bachelor's degree or greater, which is very contrary to some of the positioning that's out there and some of the understanding of this industry. About 15% have a PhD that's greater, and we have PhDs on the network earning significant amounts of money doing labeling, contributing their expertise to these models. So we've been doing expert data labeling ever since the models need it. I mean, this game is keeping in touch with the researchers, knowing what they need, coming up with ideas internally. In some ways, we drove this because we were seeing that the models were not sufficient in more expert ways. And so, we would go to the model builders and say, "Hey, we noticed that this is a problem. If you would like to fix it, this cadre of experts can do that for you." So the counter positioning is out there, but I think that's just what competitors say sometimes. It has nothing to do with reality.
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。我认为竞争对手目前的定位根本就是虚假的。首先，我会先讲一下这个，然后再稍微展开一下。我一会儿会解释我的意思。但我认为先花30秒时间讲讲Scale的历史，以及从2016年至今的发展脉络很重要。亚历克斯在很早的时候就意识到，数据对模型至关重要。当时他才19或20岁。他就想：“好吧，那我该围绕这个建立什么样的业务呢？”于是他创立了自动驾驶汽车标注业务——因为如果能标注这些数据，汽车的表现会更好。后来，这股浪潮演变为计算机视觉热潮。我们与国防部合作，为他们提供标注服务，这是在2020年。（00:14:21）接下来，随着时间推移，模型不断进步，对数据的需求也越来越高。因此，我们不断调整模型所需的数据类型。随着生成式AI浪潮兴起，整个行业也经历了巨大变革。两年前模型刚出现时，我们还记得当时它们经常产生幻觉，基本答案错误，甚至分不清哪首诗更好。那就是18个月前的标注现状。而现在，整个行业都在追求专家级数据标注，任务也越来越复杂。（00:15:15）举个例子，18个月前的情况是这样的——我到公司约13个月后，面试时看到这样的任务：给出一篇短篇小说，问“这篇比那篇好吗？”然后编辑后给出偏好排序。当时任务非常基础。尽管有一些专家涌现，但模型水平太落后，甚至连基础需求都满足不了。如今，任务难度已然翻倍：比如让全球顶尖网页开发者搭建整个网站，或者用模型解析癌症治疗中的复杂概念。这些任务耗时数小时，需要博士学位和专业人才才能完成。（00:16:01）数据支持：我们专家网络中80%的人拥有学士学位或更高学历，这与外界的认知相悖。约15%的人拥有博士学位，我们的博士专家通过标注为模型贡献专业知识。自模型诞生以来，我们就始终致力于专家级数据标注。我们与研究者保持紧密联系，内部创新思路。在某些方面，我们推动了行业进程，因为我们发现模型在更专业领域存在不足。于是我们向模型开发者提出：“嘿，我们发现这个问题。你们如果想解决，可以让这批专家来帮你们。”那些竞争对手的反驳不过是口嗨，与现实无关。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. That was extremely interesting. So what I'm hearing is yes, there has been a big shift to labs need more expert folks involved in training, labeling, writing evals. You guys are very aware of that and have evolved with that. One of the, I don't know, allegations I guess in the market is that it's hard to find these experts. So all these companies have their proprietary network of experts and how they find them. Is there anything you could share about just how you guys go about that because that feels like the hardest part is finding these experts and keeping them from other companies?
turns.zh: 好的。这非常有趣。所以我的理解是，是的，实验室确实需要更多专业人才参与培训、标注数据和撰写评估报告。你们对此非常清楚，并随之做出了调整。市场上有个说法——我也不确定是否属实——就是很难找到这些专家。因此，各家公司都有自己的专家资源库和招募渠道。能否分享一下你们是如何招募这些专家的？因为我觉得最难的部分就是找到这些专家，并防止他们被其他公司挖走。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: They are hard to find. You have to have many, many tactics. So we get, as you would expect, there's not one way you do it. The largest way is that they refer each other because when you are enjoying what you're doing and you are using your expertise to contribute to AI, which is pretty cool. If you're a PhD on this pretty specific topic and you're using a model and you're frustrated that, oh, it doesn't interact with me in the way that I want, this is a paid way to have an outlet for that and to make hundreds or thousands of dollars doing that. And so, a lot of times they refer each other. (00:18:13): We also have campus programs where we will literally go onto the campus and talk to the professors, talk to the students, ask about who would like to do this type of work. And then, of course, there's the more traditional scaled ways of LinkedIn and places like that. But the best ones come from these grassroots and referral networks. And the only way you get that is providing a great experience to these people, because these people, they're doing it partly for money, but they're also doing it because they think that their contribution to the AI models is important and interesting, and in many times it solves a problem for them.
turns.zh: 确实很难找。你得采取多种策略。正如你所料，没有一种万能的招募方法。最主要的方式是专家之间互相推荐。因为当你热爱自己的工作、能用专业知识为AI做出贡献时，这感觉很棒。如果你是一位专攻某个特定领域的博士，正在使用某个模型，却对模型无法满足你的需求感到沮丧，这就是一种既能发挥专长、又能通过此类工作赚取数百或数千美元的途径。所以很多时候他们会互相推荐。（00:18:13）我们还有校园项目，会直接去校园与教授和学生交流，询问谁愿意从事这类工作。当然，还有领英等传统招聘平台。但最优秀的人才往往来自基层推荐网络。要获得这些人才，关键在于为他们提供优质的体验，因为他们一部分是为了钱，但更多的是因为他们认为自己对AI模型的贡献既重要又有趣，而且很多时候还能解决他们自身的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So something that I've been seeing on Twitter just this week as I was preparing for this is there's the information headline. This came out and this mirrored something that Brendan from Workhorse said that over time the entire economy is going to move towards just reinforcement learning and everyone's just training AI is basically the jobs that will be left. Thoughts on that? Is that where you think things are going? Is there another perspective?
turns.zh: 这周我在为本次对话做准备时，看到推特上有个新闻标题。布伦丹在Workhorse的发言中提到，随着时间推移，整个经济将向强化学习方向发展，最终只剩下训练AI的工作。对此你怎么看？你认为事态会朝这个方向发展吗？有没有其他观点？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Reinforcement learning is very important, and I think this is a broader comment about the move to environments. There's these things called RL environments that effectively are sandboxes for AI agents to play in to accomplish a goal so that they can learn how to accomplish that goal. We've been doing this for over a year. So for example, you have a Salesforce instance. How does an AI agent navigate that instance? That instance has data that it needs to recognize, it has configurations. Salesforce is a highly configurable product. It has configurations, it needs to understand how to navigate. You're asking the agent to do a business process that needs very high reliability, and then the agent needs to know, "Hey, if I can't accomplish what I'm going to accomplish, or I think if there's a low accuracy of what I'm about to accomplish, how do I pop it up to a human being for feedback so I can get guidance?" (00:20:08): All of those things need to be trained and there's no alchemy to it. You just have to put the AI agent in an environment that represents what a human being would be doing. And you can imagine the number of environments in the world and the number of goals within each environment is enormous. So the question is, and the research that we have done over the past year to try to be a good partner to our model builders, our model builder customers, is how generalizable is each individual task or each individual environment. So if you imagine the world of environments of software systems, configurations, data types, sizes, user counts, complexities, it's like the permutations are endless. So what you need is you need a strategy that allows a lab to collect data that is generalizable enough across a broad spectrum of use cases so that they don't have to collect 45 trillion combinations of what should the agent do in this particular situation. (00:21:20): So sometimes the work and the data is highly generalizable, and by generalizable I mean you have it accomplished in a simple way. The task might be find the meeting on my calendar for my interview with Lenny, and the agent goes and it looks through all my calendar and then it pops it out, very simple example. That needs to be generalizable to any calendar search potentially or potentially any calendar action. And the more generalizable it is, the more valuable the data is. So our job is to provide the most valuable data to model builders that accomplishes the goal of making agents as useful as possible for their end users.
turns.zh: 强化学习非常重要，我认为这是一个关于环境迁移的更广泛讨论。所谓的强化学习环境实际上是AI智能体玩耍的沙盒，用于完成某个目标。过去一年来，我们一直在做这项工作。举个例子，假设你有一个Salesforce实例。AI智能体如何在该实例中导航？这个实例包含需要识别的数据和配置。Salesforce是一款高度可配置的产品，具有多样化的配置，需要智能体学会如何在其中导航。当智能体面临高可靠性的业务流程时，它需要知道：“如果我无法完成目标，或者预判完成目标的准确性过低，该如何将任务提交给人类获取反馈并获取指导？” （00:20:08）：所有这些能力都需要训练，没有什么神奇的解决方案。你只需将AI智能体置于一个能模拟人类行为的环境中。可以想象，全球环境的数量以及每个环境中目标的数量是巨大的。因此，关键问题在于——通过过去一年的研究，我们试图成为模型构建者的好伙伴——每个单独任务或每个环境的通用性有多强？想象一下软件系统环境的世界：配置、数据类型、规模、用户数量、复杂度等，这些变量组合近乎无穷无尽。因此，我们需要一种策略，让实验室能够收集在广泛用例中具有足够通用性的数据，这样他们就不必收集45万亿种组合数据，告诉智能体在特定情况下该怎么做。（00:21:20）：有时候，工作和数据的通用性很高，我说的通用性是指以简单方式完成任务。例如，智能体需要在我的日历中找到与Lenny的采访相关的会议记录，它会搜索整个日历并找到该条目，这是一个非常简单的例子。这种通用性越高，数据的价值就越大。因此，我们的职责是为模型构建者提供最有价值的数据，以实现让智能体尽可能为最终用户提供帮助的目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that you've been sharing these examples of what this stuff is specifically that these people are doing, the data you're providing to labs. So just to mirror back a few of the examples you've shared, one is an engineer building a website, sharing the code essentially with the model. And here's how I would do it. And in that example, is it just like here's the code or is it a recording of them building it? What is the data?
turns.zh: 我很高兴你分享了这些具体案例，说明人们正在做什么，以及你们为实验室提供的数据。让我回顾一下你分享的几个例子之一。一个是工程师在构建网站，本质上是与模型共享代码。然后我会这样做。在这个例子中，是直接给出代码，还是记录他们的构建过程？数据是什么？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: It could be both. So in some cases, it's just the website and here's an example, and then they design it. In some cases, it needs to be annotated in such a way that's like, I made this decision for this reason or this decision for that reason, or here's how I would think about it. So it depends on what the model builders are trying to accomplish. And so, it can get quite nuanced in terms of what they're trying to train on.
turns.zh: 两者都有可能。有些情况下，只是展示网站并给出示例，然后他们自己设计。有些情况下，需要进行注释，比如说明为什么做出这个决策，或者如何思考问题。因此，这取决于模型构建者试图训练的内容。就训练内容而言，可能会变得非常细致。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it.
turns.zh: 明白了。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: So it's not like here's a website and then it's created doing websites. It's like, here's a website, here's why I made this decision, here's why I didn't make this decision, or here's a broken website and here's why it's broken if they're trying to accomplish, I don't know, a debugging tool for a website builder or something like that.
turns.zh: 也就是说，这不像是先有网站，然后再去开发网站。更像是，先给出一个网站，接着解释自己为何做出这个决策，又为何没做出那个决策，或者展示一个故障网站，并分析其崩溃原因——假如他们的目标是为网站构建者开发一个调试工具之类的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And another example you shared is a short story where it's like, here's one short story, here's another I imagine generated by a model. And then it's like, which is better, and then how would you make it better? The other example you just shared is a Salesforce agent where it's like, Hey, book a meeting with a prospect and then teach it how that happens. I love just how concrete these are because it's like, okay, I get it. This is the stuff that these companies do. Is there another maybe one or two examples just to give people a sense of what this data looks like?
turns.zh: 你之前提到的另一个例子是短篇小说，比如先给出一篇短篇小说，再给出另一篇（我猜是模型生成的），然后比较两者的优劣，并探讨如何改进。刚刚你提到的另一个例子是Salesforce代理，用户会说"嘿，帮我预约与潜在客户的会议"，然后教它如何操作。我特别喜欢这些例子如此具体，因为这样一来就一目了然了。这些公司就是在做这些事情。能否再举一两个例子，让大家更直观地了解这些数据的具体样子？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Absolutely. I can actually give you an example from, so we have two sides of our business. One, we supply data to model builders. We sell the data, and then the other is we actually do solutions. We sell applications and services to healthcare systems, insurance systems, et cetera. I actually think it would paint a more colorful picture if I gave you an example of one of those because it involves data, but it involves the use of data, the manipulation of data for a very, very specific goal. And so, one example there is we work with a healthcare system and health systems have lots of problems. This particular healthcare system has experts that see very rare cases on a regular basis. So you go there only if no one else can figure out your problem, and there's a huge backlog. So there's a productivity element to this implementation tier. (00:24:27): So there's a huge backlog. They want to be able to see more patients, they want to be able to provide better care, and they want to prevent the number of revisits because they want to give the accurate diagnosis day one and what the treatment should be. Well, to do this today without the help of AI, the doctor really needs to read 200 to 300 pages of documentation and it's rolled into one document, but in different formats. And so, if you're a doctor, how are you going to read 200 or 300 pages of everything? So what they do is they do the best they can. They scan it, they ask a nurse to look at it, they ask maybe a more junior doctor to take a look at this case. They want to treat the patient well, obviously this is why they became a doctor. And then, they go into the room and they talk to the person and then they make a diagnosis. (00:25:14): Well, we basically built a tool that will read that document for them and point out the top 5 to 10 things that they should take into consideration, either allergies that might not be obvious is one example where we actually, we picked up on an allergy that a patient had that would not have been obvious from reading the document and that allergy actually would've had a conflict with the medication that they were going to be prescribed. And so, the AI tool basically pulled out this correlation that would've even been hard for a human being to do. To make this tool better and better, you get to a certain limit with the models off the shelf, and actually the people inside of this healthcare system have to do their own labeling. (00:25:54): So we talk about labeling for model builders, but we are starting to see the labeling move into enterprises and into governments because you can only get so far with off the shelf plus rag plus some fine-tuning based on recorded data. One thing people often miss about these systems is we assume because you hear these numbers of like, "Oh, this bank in just 200 petabytes of data a year or whatever fantastical number." What we miss is is that the right data? Which of that data is useful to the models? And most of it is not useful. Some of it is, but a lot of what we do when we're talking about knowledge work, when we're talking about making judgment is human judgment based on synthesizing how would this doctor in this case or how would this banker in this case make this decision and how would they make decision in the context of their overall enterprise? And that might be different bank to bank, healthcare system to healthcare system, because of the culture, the objectives, the incentives, et cetera. And so, we're getting to the point now where we see that digitizing judgment, human judgment, true subject matter, deep expertise is becoming a bottleneck that we're unblocking for our customers.
turns.zh:
没错。我可以举个例子来说明。我们业务分为两块：一是向建模师提供数据，我们出售这些数据；另一块是为医疗保健系统、保险系统等提供解决方案。我觉得如果能举个具体案例会更直观，因为这涉及数据，但更关键的是如何针对特定需求利用和处理数据。比如，我们与一家医疗机构合作——这类机构面临诸多难题。这家医疗机构的专家经常处理极其罕见的病例。患者往往是求助无门时才会前往，而且积压的病例数量巨大。因此，实施这些解决方案的效率至关重要。

（00:24:27）：积压的病例数量非常庞大。他们希望能诊治更多患者，提供更优质的护理，并减少复诊次数——毕竟患者需要在首次就诊时就获得准确的诊断和治疗方案。然而，在没有人工智能辅助的情况下，医生通常需要阅读200至300页的文档资料，这些资料被整合成单一文档，但格式各异。试问医生如何高效处理这些信息？他们只能尽力而为：扫描文件、请护士协助查看，或让初级医生审阅病例。他们本质上想把患者服务做好，这也是他们选择从医的初衷。随后，医生会与患者面谈并做出诊断。

（00:25:14）：我们开发的工具能自动解析这些文档，并列出需重点关注的5至10个关键信息。例如，发现患者存在隐藏的过敏反应，而这在阅读文档时可能难以察觉。AI工具能识别出这种关联性，这对人类来说并非易事。

要提升工具性能，现成模型存在局限性，医疗机构必须进行自主标注。我们为建模师提供标注工具，但目前这项技术正向企业和政府领域延伸，因为现成模型加粗糙数据的优化终有极限。人们常忽视的一个关键点是——我们仅听闻“银行每年处理200PB数据”之类的惊人数字，却忽视了核心数据的质量问题。真正有用的数据占多大比例？且多数数据并无实际价值。部分数据有用，但多数需要根据真实场景进行判断。例如，医生或银行家在特定情境下如何决策？这因机构文化、目标、激励机制等因素而异。

如今，我们正致力于将人类判断数字化、知识化，使其在企业整体框架下发挥作用。
专业知识正成为我们为客户破解的难题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's really interesting. It's like the spectrum went from just low skill generous labor to experts to now the specific expert at this one company who needs to do this work, this labeling.
turns.zh: 真有意思。这就像是技术发展历程——从低技能的体力劳动到专家，再到如今某家公司里需要处理特定任务（比如标注数据）的专业人才。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Absolutely. I mean understanding what, there's this broad narrative. We have two narratives. We have the AGI, everything is just going to become AGI, and then there's the skeptics, which is like, "Hey, this is all bunk, this is a bubble, et cetera." And of course, my view is most things are kind of like there's truth in between and some of the extreme parts of the extreme probably correct, but the reality is is that it's very hard to get machine critical use cases in agentic systems where agents are talking to agents to a level of accuracy that is necessary to accomplish a goal. And one of the main issues is that a one document, think about the problem of even understanding a document, a document that reads the exact same words in company A will have a different meaning and importance in company B. So how do you have a system that knows that? So this is all got to be built. So if you're going to make good decisions.
turns.zh: 确实如此。我的意思是，要理解这一点，我们有两种观点：一是通用人工智能（AGI）论，认为一切都会被 AGI 取代；另一是怀疑论，认为这都是胡说八道，纯粹是泡沫。当然，我认为多数情况介于两者之间，有些极端观点或许有道理，但现实是，要让智能体系统中智能体之间能够进行高精度对话以完成任务，难度极大。其中一个核心问题是，同一份文档——比如公司 A 的文档和公司 B 的文档，尽管字面内容相同，但其含义和重要性却大相径庭。那么如何让系统能理解这些差异？这都是需要逐步构建的。毕竟，要做出明智决策，这些能力缺一不可。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is a good segue to this question that is always on people's minds when they look at companies like yours and the other folks in the space is just how long do we need people to be doing this? At what point will AI be smart enough to do it themselves? I know your incentives are to say we'll never run out of people because it's aligned with your growth, but just how should we think about just why do we need people, I don't know, in 10 years? How long do we need these experts telling AI things it doesn't know?
turns.zh: 接下来要谈的是人们常问的问题：当看到像贵公司这样的企业，以及行业内其他公司时，总会想知道——我们还需要人力做多久？AI 什么时候才能足够智能，完全替代人工？我知道贵公司希望强调永远不会用尽人力，因为这与公司发展战略相符。但我们该如何看待这个问题？比如，十年后还需要人力吗？在哪些场景下，专家仍需指导 AI 完成它尚不擅长的任务？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: First off, the history of data labeling is a history of new beginnings. Autonomous vehicles do not need as much data labeling as they did in the past. I mean, Scale is a company that believes that data will always be important at the point at which you don't need external data, human data in models. I think we've gotten to a level of advancement in the world that is almost like unfathomable because you're effectively saying that no new human skill and no new human knowledge is important enough to put into these models. That feels like pretty far out there. And so, for a business like ours, we're constantly looking at how do you build operations that can constantly find the new needs and then work with the contributor network we call the experts contributors to unearth that data, to unearth that information. And sometimes it's new people, sometimes within our existing base we find that existing people have expertise that we didn't know about that maybe wasn't useful to a model a year ago, but now is useful. (00:29:47): So this is a constant progression of getting more and more data into these models. Yes, we are financially incentivized to believe that humans will always be in the loop, but that's not just a business belief, it is a personal belief. These systems need to work for us, and if these systems work for us, then we will need to be on the loop or in the loop on any of the decisions that these systems make. As to the broader point around labor, which I think comes up around white collar apocalypse and these things that come up, I'm definitely on the more maybe practical side of this, possibly just because of my nature, possibly because I see what's going on on the ground actually in these customers where supposedly this transformation is going to happen in the next one to two years. And I just think that it might happen. The space is moving super fast, but I don't think it's going to happen. (00:30:39): It is definitely not going to happen in the next year. The idea that it happens in the next two years I think is very far-fetched, but nothing's impossible here. And long-term, I think that if you go back through, I don't know, pessimist archive or whatever, these accounts that post, the radio was invented and then all of this will be eliminated. There will be change, but the change, I think humans are very good at adapting. So I think what we're underestimating in all of the doom and gloom is we believe in human adaptability. We as a company are highly adaptable and I think the history of technology has shown that people are adaptable.
turns.zh: 首先，数据标注的历史就是一个不断创新的过程。自动驾驶汽车现在对数据标注的需求比过去要低得多。我想说，Scale公司认为，当你不再需要外部数据、不再需要人类数据来构建模型时，数据将始终至关重要。我认为我们已经达到了一个几乎令人难以置信的进步阶段，因为你实际上是在说，不需要新的人类技能，也不需要新的人类知识来输入这些模型。这感觉实在是太不可思议了。因此，对于我们这样的公司来说，我们一直在思考如何建立一个能够不断发现新需求的运营体系，然后与我们称之为"专家贡献者"的贡献者网络合作，挖掘这些数据和信息。有时是新人，有时是在我们现有的用户群中发现一些原本不被视为对模型有用、但现在却变得有用的专业知识。（00:29:47）：因此，将越来越多的数据输入这些模型是一个持续的进程。是的，我们出于商业动机相信人类将始终参与其中，但这不仅仅是一种商业信念，更是一种个人信念。这些系统必须为我们服务，如果这些系统为我们服务，那么我们就需要参与到这些系统所做出的任何决策中去。至于更广泛的劳动力问题，我认为这涉及到"白领末日论"之类的话题，我对此持更务实的态度，可能只是因为我的性格，也可能是因为我实际看到客户端正在发生的事情——据称这种转型将在未来一到两年内发生。但我认为这不太可能发生。（00:30:39）：明年肯定不会发生。我认为未来两年内发生这种情况的可能性微乎其微，但一切皆有可能。从长远来看，如果你回顾那些悲观主义者的言论，比如认为无线电的发明会导致所有这些东西被淘汰之类的，我认为这些观点都太离谱了。变革肯定会发生，但我认为人类非常善于适应变化。所以我认为，在所有悲观论调中，我们低估了人类的适应能力。我们公司本身就具有很强的适应性，而技术史也表明，人类确实有很强的适应能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really like that takeaway. I'm an optimist as well, so I'm always looking for reasons to be optimistic. I want to follow that thread before I get there, something very tactical I want to ask about is evals seems to be coming up a lot, especially with companies in your space. I'm still learning a lot about just what this all is, especially in your market. How much of what you or experts are providing are evals versus other types of data?
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢这种观点。作为一个乐观主义者，我也一直在寻找乐观的理由。在深入探讨之前，我想先问一个比较实际的问题——评估（evals）似乎经常被提及，尤其是在你们所在的行业。我还在深入了解这一切，尤其是你们的市场。你们或专家提供的数据中，评估占了多大比例？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: A lot of it's evals, and within enterprise customers and government customers, it's mostly evals because somebody's got to establish the benchmark for what good looks like. That's the simple way to think about evals. What does good look like and do you have a comprehensive set of evals so that the system knows what good looks like? It's as simple as that.
turns.zh: 大部分都是评估。在企业客户和政府客户中，评估占了绝大多数，因为总得有人为"优秀"的标准设定基准。这就是评估的简单理解——什么才算优秀？你是否有全面的评估体系，让系统知道什么才算优秀？就是这么简单。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So in the case maybe of the healthcare example you shared, essentially this doctor would be sitting there looking at all these reports, creating evals that are like, this is what this should be discovering in this report, in this record. Is that a way to think about it?
turns.zh: 好的，回到你提到的医疗案例。基本上，医生需要坐在那里查看所有报告，制定评估标准，比如“这份报告应该能发现哪些问题？”或者“这个记录里有什么异常？”对此你怎么看？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Yeah, that's a very big part of it, which is what does good look like?
turns.zh: 是的，这其中很重要的一点是，什么才算“优秀”？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome, okay.
turns.zh: 太棒了，好的。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: I have to reduce things down to simple terms.
turns.zh: 我得把这些概念简化成通俗易懂的术语。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting you say good versus correct. Is that a specific term you like to use good versus just this is the correct answer.
turns.zh: 你提到“优秀”和“正确”，这很有意思。这里“优秀”和“正确”是特定的术语吗？你更倾向于用“优秀”来强调人机协作的价值？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: I didn't intentionally use that word, but these are probabilistic systems and so depending upon... Yeah, so I can get into some nuance here about the right types of problems that AI is good at solving. So if you have a human process that is 10 or 20% accurate or 10 or 20% liked, AI is awesome. Because if you get to 50, 60, 70, 80% accurate, you're in the money, you're in the green, everybody's happy. Now, the system then has to know, hey, for the remainder, how do I make sure that humans are involved for the remainder of the decision making? But from a net value add standpoint, the humans are pumped in that scenario. (00:33:13): If you have a human process, a workflow that is 98% accurate, and you expect an AI system to get you the remaining 2%, not totally there yet. And so, when I say what does good look like? A lot of the processes and a lot of the things that people are asking these systems to do and systems for us to build are making judgments on their behalf. And so, just like we would ask a human being, "Hey, what do you think we should do in this scenario?" What you're looking for is you're looking for the best recommendation or course of action given the current information.
turns.zh: 我倒没刻意用这个词，但概率系统本质上是基于概率运算的。所以关键在于，如何判断哪些问题适合AI处理？比如，如果一个人工流程的准确率只有10%或20%，但AI能提升到50%、60%、70%、80%，那就是成功了。这时候系统需要考虑：剩余的决策环节如何确保人类参与？但从整体价值创造的角度看，人类在这种场景下会非常兴奋。（00:33:13）：如果人工流程的准确率达到98%，而期望AI能完成剩余的2%工作，这就有点不切实际了。所以我问“优秀是什么样子的？”时，很多流程和人们要求AI完成的任务，本质上都是在替人类做判断。比如我们会问一个人：“在这种情况下，你觉得应该怎么做？”你要找的是给定当前信息下，最优的建议或行动方案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To you, this is so obvious and to people in your market that I think a lot of people think about AI being trained on just here's a bunch of data, check it out, learn everything you can from all of human history and all of written record. But what's wild is basically people are sitting around teaching AI things it doesn't know, filling gaps. That's how AI is getting smarter now. There's no more real data for it to feed on. It's just like, here's what I don't know, or here's what an expert found you're wrong. I'm going to teach you this. And the fact that it scales and that's keeping models improving is so mind-boggling.
turns.zh: 在你看来，这很显而易见，但对你的市场参与者来说，很多人认为AI就是拿一堆数据去训练，学习人类历史和书面记录中的所有知识。但令人惊讶的是，人们现在主要是在教AI它不知道的东西，填补知识空白。这就是AI现在能不断进步的原因。现在没有更多真实数据可供训练了，更多的是“我不知道这个，或者专家发现你错了，我来教你这个”。而这种扩展性和模型持续改进的能力实在令人惊叹。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Yes. No, yeah, I agree. I mean, like with any of these major tech revolutions, the headlines tell one story and then on the ground, laying broadband means you need to dig up every single road in America to lay it. There is the, yeah, it's as simple as that. Someone's got to dig up the road or someone's got to run the undersea cable. There's always some operational chiseling that's going on in all of these industries. I mean, if you think about how magical these models are, they're remarkable that if you've been in technology long enough, it blows my mind even today that they get the punctuation right consistently. I mean, that sounds like almost daft to say at this point in the market, but if you were to go back three years and think about that from a technological standpoint, a lot of things that we think are trivial now are very sophisticated, and it's a combination of, I mean, the real answer is it's a combination of computational power, model improvement, and data, and all three are getting better at once.
turns.zh: 是的。不，嗯，我同意你的看法。我是说，像任何重大科技革命一样，头条新闻讲的是一个故事，但现实情况是，要在美国铺设宽带网络，就得把每条道路都挖开。这就是现实，嗯，就是这么简单。总得有人挖开道路，或者铺设海底光缆。所有这些行业都在不断进行着实际操作层面的调整。我是说，如果你回想一下这些模型的神奇之处——如果你在科技行业待得够久，至今它们能始终正确使用标点符号这一点仍让我感到惊讶。在当前市场环境下这么说或许听起来有点荒谬，但如果你回溯三年前，从技术角度来看，如今我们视为理所当然的许多事情都曾非常复杂。这是计算能力、模型改进和数据三者协同作用的结果，而这三者目前都在同步提升。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's follow that thread. You've been at Scale for a long time, CEO for, you said, 13 months. I feel like you see a lot more about where things are heading because you work with labs on things they haven't even announced yet. You see more than most people, and I know there's only so much you can share about what companies are doing, but just is there anything you think people don't truly grasp or understand about where AI models are going to be in the next two, three years?
turns.zh: 接下来谈谈你对 Scale 的看法。你在 Scale 工作了很久，担任 CEO 才 13 个月。我觉得你对行业发展方向有更深刻的洞察，因为你与实验室合作开发尚未公布的项目。你比大多数人更能预见未来——当然，关于公司机密你不能透露太多，但你能否谈谈人们对未来两三年内 AI 模型发展方向的误解或不解之处？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Look, there's so much talk. I think it depends on how much X or news you consume. So I think it's like what sort of our perspective. The general trend right now is going from models knowing things to models doing things. And we're pushing the boundaries of knowledge, like the benchmarks that we put out and that others put out are showing that the knowledge that these models have is getting, it's quite robust. And then, the next question becomes, well, what can it do for me? And as soon as you get into that world, that's where the environments we were talking about start to come into play. How do you navigate a Salesforce instance? How do you navigate a healthcare system? How do you navigate even a weather app on your phone, and how does the agent make decisions for you? (00:36:36): We're just getting into the beginning of that. It'll be very interesting to see how quickly that happens. And I think that's where a lot of the speculation has a wide variance because we're at the beginning of it. People take different trajectories on how that's going to improve. And so, if you take a trajectory of the most aggressive trajectory, which is like, oh, it's actually going to be quite easy to train on these things, and then it's just a change management exercise in the economy, which by the way, change management exercises are not to be underestimated. (00:37:06): There's still people in the world without an email address. And so, the adoption curve then becomes a human and policy issue, not a technological issue. We're not there from the technology standpoint, but I do think in the next two to three years, if I take the bait and have to make a guess is the technology will get to a point where it will push the change management and policy makers to say like, "Oh, what do we do with this because it's getting pretty close?" That's probably two or three years away.
turns.zh: 看，这方面的讨论太多了。我认为这取决于你接触了多少 X 技术或新闻。所以我的观点是，当前大趋势是从模型「知晓」转向模型「行动」。我们正在突破知识边界，比如我们发布的基准测试和其他机构发布的基准测试都表明，这些模型的知识储备已经相当丰富。接下来问题就是，它能为我做什么？一旦进入这个领域，我们之前讨论的环境因素就开始发挥作用了。比如如何导航 Salesforce 实例？如何导航医疗系统？甚至如何使用手机天气应用，以及智能助手如何为你做决策？（00:36:36）：我们才刚刚踏入这个领域。观察其发展速度会非常有趣。我认为这正是当前诸多猜测存在巨大分歧的原因——毕竟我们才刚刚起步。人们对其改进路径有着不同的预测。就最乐观的情况而言，训练这些模型会变得相当容易，然后在经济层面只需进行变革管理。但说实话，这类变革管理工作不容小觑。（00:37:06）：世界上仍有很多人没有电子邮箱。所以采用曲线就成了人力和政策问题，而非技术问题。从技术角度看，我们尚未达到那个阶段，但我确实认为在未来两到三年内，如果我大胆猜测，技术将发展到迫使变革管理者和政策制定者不得不说「哦，我们该怎么处理这个问题，因为它已经快要实现了」的地步。可能还需要两到三年的时间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's been a lot of talk these days about AI not delivering on the promise that we hear, especially at enterprises. There's this MIT study that just showed that there's all these pilots that people are excited about and then they don't work and companies aren't adopting these tools. There's data showing engineers are not actually as productive with tools. It actually slows them down sometimes. You work with a ton of companies implementing all kinds of AI. What are you seeing on the ground? What kind of gains are you seeing? Do you feel like it's overhyped, underhyped?
turns.zh: 最近有很多关于人工智能未能兑现承诺的讨论，尤其是在企业层面。麻省理工学院的一项研究显示，许多试点项目虽然最初备受期待，但最终却未能成功，企业也未能广泛采用这些工具。还有数据显示，工程师使用这些工具后的生产力实际上并未提升，有时甚至会拖慢他们的工作进度。你与众多实施各类人工智能项目的公司合作过。在实际应用中，你观察到了哪些情况？看到了哪些成效？你觉得这项技术是被过度炒作了，还是被低估了？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: There's a lot of hype out there, and our job is to actually build products that work, that deliver value for our customers and figure out where the rubber hits the road. And to get a sophisticated, my healthcare example is one, we do other sophisticated workflows, claims management for insurance companies. This is a financial decision that's happening, but it's an automatable process. But basically what happens is the POCs get to 60 or 70% of the way there, and the human mind goes, oh, the rest is no big deal. But it's like uptime in data centers where every nine is an order of magnitude investment in terms of reliability, backups, et cetera. One nine is basically a web server in a dorm room like we had at UCLA, and then five nines is this crazy high bar, but it just seems like a very small movement. (00:38:55): So you have a similar dynamic going on here where you have a bunch of people, one of the reasons why the POCs have failed, one, there's a denominator effect because it's so easy to do, "Hey, I spun up a project, I spun up a project, I spun up a project." So it's really easy for people to try. So I don't necessarily know that the 95% number, I think is a bit of clickbait in a way. It tells the right story, but it is a little bit hyperbolic because if you take the efforts that happen in the company where they actually get a quality partner like we are, or if you do it yourself, if you have engineers who've worked with models before and they put in the time, and I'm talking about months, not like minutes like you see in these videos to actually get legal approval, policy approval, regulatory approval, change managements like an accuracy that everybody's comfortable with. If you actually do that, these things take 6 to 12 months to get them truly robust enough where an important process can be automated. (00:40:00): So I think that's where the hype is right that when you do it, the impact is like, whoa, I never would've figured that out myself, and I'm one of the most educated doctors in the world as an example. But the time to get there is just longer than what people are selling.
turns.zh: 市面上有很多宣传，但我们的职责是真正开发出能为客户创造价值的产品，弄清楚关键难点所在。比如在医疗领域，我们处理复杂的工作流程，比如保险公司的理赔管理。这涉及财务决策，但本质上是一个可自动化的流程。但现实情况是，试点项目往往推进到60%或70%时，人们就觉得剩下的部分不难了。但就像数据中心的可用性要求，每增加一个9，意味着在可靠性、备份等方面的投资要增加一个数量级。一个9对应的是像UCLA宿舍里的web服务器，而五个9则代表着极高的标准，但人们往往觉得这只是微小的进步。（00:38:55）：在人工智能项目中也存在类似的现象。试点项目失败的原因之一是，门槛过低导致试错成本过低。“嘿，我启动了一个项目，又启动了一个项目。”人们很容易尝试。但我不确定95%的成功率是否准确，感觉有点吸引眼球。数据听起来不错，但其实有些夸大其词。比如在企业中，要想真正找到优质合作伙伴，比如我们这样的公司，或者自己动手开发，工程师需要投入数月时间——而不是视频里几分钟就能完成——才能获得法律许可、政策批准、监管审批，完成变更管理，最终让模型达到大家都认可的准确度。这些步骤需要6到12个月才能让重要流程实现自动化。（00:40:00）：所以我认为宣传和实际效果之间的落差确实存在。当你真正应用时，那种惊喜感会让人感叹：“我自己绝对想不到能做到这样。” 我可是全球最顶尖的医生之一。但要达到这个水平，所需的时间远超人们宣传的程度。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's such a good point that it's not only is it easy to try these things, it's just like everyone's doing it so everyone's feeling FOMO like, "I got to try these things. I got to try all these prototyping tools, Cursor, all these things." Just goes, "Everyone's doing it," and then you just rush into it and it doesn't actually work out.
turns.zh: 一个很重要的观点是，这些技术不仅易于尝试，而且因为大家都在做，导致人们产生了“错失恐惧症”，比如“我得试试这些原型工具，Cursor之类的。” 然后就盲目投入，结果却不尽如人意。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Easy to learn, hard to master. That's my summary.
turns.zh: 学起来容易，掌握起来难。这就是我的总结。
