turns.zh: 本期节目由Mercury赞助。我在Mercury开户多年了，说实话，现在我已经无法想象还有其他银行能提供如此便捷的服务了。我从Chase银行转过来后，天壤之别。转账、追踪消费记录、授权团队成员调配资金，这些操作简直轻而易举。相比之下，大多数传统银行网站和应用界面繁琐难用，而Mercury的设计堪称精益求精，操作直观流畅。Mercury将您使用资金的所有场景整合到一个产品中，包括信用卡、发票管理、账单支付、团队报销以及资本融资等功能。（00:41:11）：无论您是资金充足的科技初创公司，正在寻找支付承包商和闲置资金增值的解决方案；还是需要向客户开具发票并保持收款进度的代理机构；抑或需要实时监控现金流和获取资金支持的电商品牌，Mercury都能量身定制服务，助力您的业务达到新高度。欢迎体验20万+创业者信赖的Mercury服务。访问mercury.com，10分钟即可在线申请。Mercury是一家金融科技公司，并非传统银行。银行服务由Mercury的联邦存款保险公司（FDIC）承保的合作银行提供。更多详情请查看节目笔记。（00:41:44）：好的，让我们转回正题。关于人工智能的讨论可以无止境地延续，但您还有更多经验值得分享。您参与过Uber Eats的建设，曾创办过多家初创公司。我们之前还聊过Scour。多年来与您共事过的许多人让我深刻领悟到您在某些领域的卓越才能。接下来我会逐一剖析其中的精髓。首先，您对贴近客户、倾听客户需求的执着令人赞叹。谈及这个话题时，我总会想起很多人自诩擅长此道，却又缺乏深刻理解。大家都觉得自己做得不错，认为这无关紧要。殊不知其他人不做，而您却在践行。您能否分享一下，当您把这项工作做得极致时，旁人眼中会如何评价其重要性？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: I mean, I probably fall in the category of what you just described, which is maybe part of the hubris you need to start anything new. But I mean, I don't think it's a clean process. I think my process is I'm constantly questioning every single thing that I'm hearing at the beginning of anything. I don't take what a customer says literally. And there's been a lot talked about on this topic from a product management standpoint in terms of like, oh, don't do what they say, do what they mean, and look at the real problems and underlying things. I think the way that I look at it that might be additive to the discussion is I look at the underlying incentives of the customer. And the underlying incentives of customers are not always financial. Sometimes it's ego, sometimes it's career growth. (00:43:24): If you're selling enterprise software to someone, there's an executive sponsor as an example, that person needs to trust that you're going to do a good job for them. How do you get them to jump with you on this big project? Well, that's part of the journey of not just the product, but what do they need to hear from us? What do we need to supply them? What do we need to do to actually unlock the opportunity to implement the product? So I think there's an incentives alignment baseline. I'm a big believer that it's cliche, but show me the incentive and I'll show you the outcome. I think that's absolutely true. And even when customers will tell you things, I'll give you an example. I've been out of the game for a while so I can be open about it, Uber Eats. (00:44:06): So when we launched Uber Eats, I looked at the business in terms of being close to the customer. We actually couldn't get a restaurant tour. I knew nothing about this industry. So at Uber, my job was to figure out what other businesses we should get into. And so, we looked at a billion businesses and Uber Eats, food delivery was the one that we thought was most interesting, which turned out to be right so good for us.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，我可能属于你刚刚描述的那种类型，这或许正是你要开展新事业所需的那种傲慢。但我认为这并非一个清晰的过程。我的方法是，在任何新事物开始之初，我都会不断质疑所听到的每件事。我不会字面理解客户所说的话。关于这个话题，从产品管理的角度已经有很多讨论，比如，别按字面意思做，要理解客户的真正意图，关注真正的问题和深层需求。我认为我看待这个问题的角度可能对讨论有所补充——我会审视客户的深层动机。客户的深层动机并不总是金钱。有时是虚荣心，有时是职业发展。（00:43:24）：如果你向某人销售企业软件，比如说有一个高管赞助者，这个人需要相信你能为他们做好工作。如何让他们与你共同参与这个大项目？这不仅关乎产品本身，还关乎我们需要向他们传达什么信息？我们需要为他们提供什么？我们需要做些什么才能真正释放实施产品的机遇？所以我认为存在一个动机匹配的基准。我深信这虽然是老生常谈，但“给我看动机，我就能告诉你结果”这句话千真万确。即使客户告诉你一些事情，我举个例子。我离开这个行业有一段时间了，所以可以坦率地说说Uber Eats。（00:44:06）：当我们推出Uber Eats时，我从贴近客户的角度审视这个业务。我们甚至无法获得餐厅考察的机会。我对这个行业一无所知。所以在Uber，我的任务是研究我们应该进军哪些其他业务。于是，我们考察了数千个行业，最终认为Uber Eats（外卖配送）最有趣，事实证明这个选择是对的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Very right.
turns.zh: 太对了。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: And we couldn't get a restaurant tour to help us understand their unit economics. And they'd say like, "Oh, it'd be this percentage or that percentage, or Why do you want to know?" And then we'd go to a different restaurant tour and they would explain it, but they were a little suspicious of why are these Uber guys talking to me about how much my ham costs? And so, what we did is we ordered just a bunch of food from these places, and then we got a restaurant supplier to give us a base catalog, and we just matched up how much does the ham weigh? How much does the cheese weigh? How much does the bread weigh? How many pieces of lettuce were on there? And we tried to actually just compose our own independent view of what's the ingredients cost versus what's the labor cost? And then, we triangulated what was our ground truth, and then what are we being told by restaurant tours, and then what is the site guys telling us about restaurant economics? (00:45:16): And if those things all overlapped, and we're like, okay, we have an insight about what to do here and how does this relate to Uber Eats? Well, what we found as part of this is that roughly a restaurant pays 20 to 30% of every meal to ingredients, and they pay roughly 20 or 30% to labor, and they pay roughly 10% to real estate and a bunch of other, anyway, so goes down the chain. But the important parts is what's the value of incrementality? (00:45:41): And so, we came in and we said, "We're going to charge you 30% of the bill." And they were like, "Oh my God, is this group on all over again? This is way too high. Oh my gosh." And we explained the economics to them and they were like, "Okay, we'll give it a try, but this is way too high." And they were right, the real number, the real clearing prices aren't 25%, but we weren't that far off. And so, when you go to find product market fit or be close to the customers, it's a combination of what's the most valuable thing. Well, in a restaurant tours case, give me incremental demand. Because if you were to take a restaurant location and triple demand based on the same labor but you're just scaling ingredients, you've got a 70, 80% incremental gross margin product. (00:46:27): Restaurant tours would hate when we would say this because it doesn't work out exactly like that in reality. But because we had that insight, we had confidence that we could go to market with, we need to charge you this so that the delivery fee can be that. And then, if the delivery fee is that and we charge you this, then we think the consumers will adopt, and that's what you need to get your incremental demand, and then we could pay the driver this. And so, you fit this whole puzzle together without totally satisfying, in the case of a marketplace, you're not totally satisfying any individuals 100% of their needs. What you're satisfying is is you're getting a clearing rate for them to participate in the market in the case of a marketplace. So that's one example.
turns.zh: 然而，我们没能获得餐厅参观的机会来帮助我们理解他们的单位经济效益。他们会说类似的话，比如：“哦，那个百分比是多少，或者你为什么想知道？”然后我们去参加另一个餐厅参观，他们会解释，但他们对“优步的人为什么要问我火腿价格”这类问题心存疑虑。于是，我们从这些餐厅订购了一堆食物，然后让餐厅供应商给我们一份基础目录，计算火腿的重量、奶酪的重量、面包的重量，以及生菜片的数量。我们试图独立评估食材成本和劳动力成本之间的关系，然后将这些数据与餐厅参观提供的信息以及优步外卖团队提供的餐厅经济学数据进行三角验证。（00:45:16）：如果这些数据吻合，我们就能理解优步外卖的商业逻辑了。我们发现，大多数餐厅将餐费的20%至30%用于食材，20%至30%用于劳动力，10%用于房租等其他成本。利润分成比例会随着供应链环节的深入而降低。但关键问题在于增量价值有多大？（00:45:41）：我们提议向餐厅收取30%的佣金时，他们惊呼：“天哪，这些人又来了。这也太高了！”。我们向他们解释了经济学原理，他们才勉强接受，但佣金比例确实偏高。实际佣金比例并非25%，但我们的估算也相差不远。寻找产品市场匹配点或贴近客户需求，需要关注最有价值的部分。就餐厅参观业务而言，关键在于获取增量需求。例如，如果能将现有餐厅位置的客流量提升三倍，仅增加食材成本而保持劳动力成本不变，产品毛利率就能达到70%至80%。（00:46:27）：餐厅参观者对此很不满，因为现实中并非完全如此。但凭借这些洞察，我们有信心推向市场：我们需要收取这样的佣金，才能覆盖配送成本。若设定这样的佣金，再加上合理的配送费，我们相信消费者会接受。这样就能拼凑出整个商业模式的拼图。虽然在平台经济中，永远无法完全满足每个用户的需求，但至少能为他们提供参与市场的合理回报。这只是一个案例。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I love this example as you almost you figure out how to help them with something they don't even fully themselves know yet. So as you think through their goals for them as if you were them, break down the economics and then here's the solution versus, hey, what can we do for you guys?
turns.zh: 是啊。我很喜欢这个案例，因为你几乎能帮他们解决他们自己尚未完全意识到的问题。换位思考他们的目标，拆解经济学模型，然后给出解决方案，而不是简单地问“我们能为你们做些什么？”。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, if you walked into a restaurant, they would tell you a bunch of things. They would say, "Oh, labor schedule is an issue." They would say, "My rent is an issue." They would say, "All these, my ingredients prices are an issue, that's 20 or 30%." If you could shave off 3% of that, that would be huge. You might then take that and go, "I'm going to go build a business. It's going to save you 10% of your ingredients costs." (00:47:45): Well, but that doesn't actually get into their head on what's truly important day-to-day. That might be important for them on an annual basis, but on a daily basis, what are they doing? They're looking at their numbers, they're looking do people show up. Did I make money yesterday? Am I going to make money tomorrow? So the urgency, I think the biggest thing people miss when they're building new products is the urgency of the buyer part of it. You can build something that provides a lot of value, but if it's not the top thing that the customer is thinking about in their busy days, then you're just going to have a long road to a small town.
turns.zh: 是啊。我是说，如果你走进一家餐厅，他们会跟你说一堆问题。他们会说：“哦，员工排班是个问题。”他们会说：“我的房租是个问题。”他们会说：“所有这些，我的食材价格是个问题，占成本的20%到30%。”如果你能削减3%的成本，那可真是笔大收获。然后你可能会想：“我要去创业。这样能帮你节省10%的食材成本。”（00:47:45）：不过这并不能让他们真正理解日常经营的核心问题。这些问题对他们来说可能是年度层面的，但日常工作中，他们关注的是什么？他们看的是财务数据，看有没有顾客光临。昨天赚了钱吗？明天能赚到钱吗？所以我觉得，开发新产品时最容易被忽视的一点就是买家的紧迫感。你可以开发出极具价值的产品，但如果这不是客户在忙碌生活中最关心的头等大事，那你注定要在漫长而曲折的道路上艰难前行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This touches on just the theme I heard a lot about, this idea of independent thinking and how much you value that, and this feels like a really good example of that. Is there anything else along those lines of just why this way of thinking is so critical?
turns.zh: 这正好触及了我常听到的一个主题——独立思考的重要性，以及人们对它的重视程度。这种案例真是绝佳的例证。还有没有其他类似的例子，能说明为什么这种思维方式如此关键？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: I think as a founder's job, and I mean I stretched that term because at Uber we had all of the benefits of Uber so I wasn't really a founder. I just started the business there. But there are some elements of founding there is you're looking for alpha in the market. When we started our first company in '97, it wasn't that cool. It might've been cool in Silicon Valley, but it was definitely not cool in LA. Now, it's super cool to start a business. So as a result, everyone's trying everything. So how do you get alpha on that market. If your research is highly influenced by what the world is saying around you, you're not going to have an independent insight. You have to go off and do your own thing. (00:49:14): And this is why from an entrepreneurship standpoint, I have very strong feelings about what the approach to founding a company should be and is probably very particular to me. But it truly is about what insight do I have, because why am I so lucky to have this insight? Why in a world of a million entrepreneurs who are thinking, who are smart, who are trying everything, why am I in the position where I likely have an insight that others do not? And then, why am I the one to do it? (00:49:46): And the answer might be I'm in this narrow, far-flung place. The other answer might be, I am inherently a contrarian personality type, so I'm just constantly looking for the thing that's true that people don't believe is true, which sometimes worked. But then, the second part of that's super important, which is why do I want to work on this problem for 5 to 10 years? And people get this wrong all the time. They go and talk to a customer and they go, "They have a problem. I'm going to go solve it." And it's just not a great way to start a business. You really have to have this burning desire to constantly be questioning yourself. (00:50:20): The other thing about independent thinking is is that you can't fall in love with your ideas. And I do not proclaim to be the world's greatest thinker for what it's worth, this is what you've been told, but is just part of that is basically throwing away who you are, who you've been, all your ideas for the mission that you're on, which is trying to accomplish something for our customer.
turns.zh:
我认为，作为创始人，我得说这个称呼用得有些宽泛，因为在优步，我享有优步带来的种种好处，所以严格来说我算不上真正的创始人，我只是在那里创办了公司。但创始人工作的确有一些核心要素——比如在市场中寻找先机。1997年我们创办第一家公司时，那可不算酷。即便在硅谷可能还算热门，但在洛杉矶绝对不受待见。如今创业已然成了时髦事物。因此，每个人都在尝试各种模式。但如何在市场中找到先机呢？如果你对市场的判断深受外界声音影响，就永远无法形成独立见解。你必须坚持自己的方向。

（00:49:14）这就是为什么从创业视角来看，我对创办公司的方法有着强烈的看法，而且这些观点可能对我个人而言独到。但归根结底，关键在于我能否洞察到真相。为什么我能幸运地获得这些洞见？在数百万个正在思考、聪明且尝试各种方法的创业者中，我为何能占据这个位置？而我又为何要亲自去做这件事？

（00:49:46）答案或许是我身处这个狭窄而偏远的领域。另一个答案可能是，我天生就是个逆向投资者，总是去寻找那些人们不愿相信的事实，有时这确实奏效。但更重要的是，我为什么要花5到10年时间专注于这个问题？人们常把这部分搞错。他们去和客户交谈，说：“他们有问题，我要去解决它。”但这绝不是创业的正确方式。你必须要有这种持续质疑自己的强烈渴望。

（00:50:20）关于独立思考的另一个要点是，不能沉溺于自己的想法。说实话，我并不自诩是世界上最伟大的思想家，但关键在于，要为手头的任务抛弃过去的自己、过去的想法，这需要你为客户创造价值的使命感。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is great. I'm glad you went here. This touches on the other theme I heard often about you is just how high of a bar you set for new businesses. And I think this advice is useful both for founders, as you said, and also people starting companies within companies, new business lines. So you've talked about this a bit already, but is there anything more there, just how high that bar needs to be for it to likely work out when you're starting something new?
turns.zh: 这太棒了。很高兴你能来分享。这让我想起我常听到的另一个关于你的特质——你对新业务设定了极高的标准。我觉得这种建议对创始人很有用，也适用于在公司内部创办新业务或新部门的人。所以你已经讲过一些，但有没有更深入的见解？当你开创新事业时，标准究竟要设得多高才能成功？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Look, if you want to give yourself the best chance, and this isn't always how it works, but if you're in my position 25 plus years in their career, if you want to give yourself the best chance, I think there's two ways that companies end up working out. And the first way, which is probably the most important, quite frankly, is that the founder is just a force of nature over a long duration of time. Because you're going to have to pivot, you have to have that energy to pivot. You have to go years and years and years with it being hard, and that's probably the most important thing. (00:51:36): But the second most important thing is that you can easily educate yourself on what are good business models, what are bad business models, what are good markets, what are bad markets? And even if you're this force of nature, having the knowledge, if you're going to go into a bad market with all your energy, you should at least know, maybe ignorance is bliss because you just throw yourself into it and it just works out with time. But that's not how I would operate, which is marketplaces are good businesses. SaaS, at least historically, we'll see how this changes, but SaaS, historically, great businesses, recurring revenue businesses, sticky businesses, network effect businesses. (00:52:12): And if you look at what the top VCs invest in, yes, there is a lot of portfolio building, but there are similarities in terms of the types of business models that they believe could be worth tens of billions of dollars. And they have network effects, they have lock-in. They are more valuable at scale, a big scale than low scale. So if you just take a filter on a new business, this is what I did at Uber, which is like if you just have a filtering mechanism on a new business, it doesn't take that long to eliminate the bad ideas. And then, of what's left, you can pick, oh, I'm very passionate about this, even though it might have more problems than this other thing that on paper looks better. And then, you have to have passionate about it. But I think people just miss a basic understanding of what businesses even have a chance of being worth $100 billion.
turns.zh: 听着，如果你想给自己争取最大的成功机会——虽然现实并非总是如此，但如果你处在我这样拥有25年以上从业经验的位置——我认为有两种方法能让公司最终取得成功。首先，也是最重要的一点，是创始人必须是一股持久的推动力。因为你必须能灵活调整策略，必须有这样的能量去应对挑战。你必须在困难重重的岁月里坚持不懈，而这或许是最关键的因素。（00:51:36）但第二个同样重要的因素是，你要能有效学习，了解哪些商业模式是优秀的，哪些是糟糕的，哪些市场有潜力，哪些市场注定失败。即便你天赋异禀，如果贸然进入一个糟糕的市场，光凭热情也未必能成功。或许无知者无畏，蒙眼狂奔终有回报，但这绝非我的处世之道。市场平台类业务才是优质选择。SaaS模式，至少从历史经验来看（未来尚待观察），始终是成功的典范——它们具有复发性收入、用户粘性、网络效应等核心特质。（00:52:12）看看顶级风投机构的投资方向，虽然多元布局是必然趋势，但他们对具备数百亿美元价值潜力的商业模式有着相似的共识——这些模式必须具备网络效应和用户锁定特性，大规模运营比小规模更具价值。以Uber为例，我曾采用过一种筛选机制：先快速排除不靠谱的想法，再从剩余选项中挑选出那些虽存在更多挑战，但我真正充满热情的项目。归根结底，关键在于对商业本质的深刻洞察——哪些行业真正有机会诞生千亿美元级巨头。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you launched Uber Eats, you figured out this is the place to go and bet. As an outsider, feels obvious, of course this is going to be a massive success. Of course, food delivery, such a good idea. I know you looked at a ton of ideas in that process. Can you just talk about what you explored and why you ended up picking Uber Eats?
turns.zh: 那么你推出了Uber Eats，认为这是值得押注的方向。作为局外人，这一选择看似显而易见——食品配送无疑是个绝佳的赛道。你肯定在此过程中考察过大量创意，能否谈谈你探索过的方向，以及为何最终选择Uber Eats？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: I am definitely not the smartest person in the room when it comes to figuring these things out. And so, I keep a very, very wide aperture on ideas for as long as I can until I'm like, okay, everything is coalescing. And I think there's a bunch of reasons why you have to keep an open aperture on considering ideas that might seem bad at the start, but you just keep digging and see if you're right that they're bad or you're wrong. So just as a general philosophical principle, I'll start there. We looked at, we did some crazy stuff. I went walking around San Francisco one day and I looked down Market Street and there was a CVS, a 7-Eleven, a CVS, a Walgreens, a 7-Eleven, and I'm like, "How many SKUs could possibly be inside one of these things that people want and couldn't you just put that into a van and you hit the button on the van and the van comes around and you get whatever convenience items you have, and they're convenience items, so why would that be a problem?" (00:54:14): And we launched that in DC. We put 10 of these trucks on the road, we put 250 SKUs in them. And I mean, crickets is an understatement of how bad it was. I mean, we couldn't get an order to save our lives. And what we realized was that we hadn't really done the research on what convenience stores really were. It was if you didn't have cigarettes, you didn't have beer, you didn't have Slurpees, you didn't have these things, for example, you didn't bring people in to sell all the other things. So we didn't know anything about retail. We were clueless. So that's one idea. We looked at grocery, but honestly the unit economics just terrified me of all the pick packing and everything like that. I think Instacart did a remarkably good job at getting the unit economics to a good spot and probably the hardest operational problem you could tackle. (00:54:56): We did generalized delivery, point to point delivery, what's now, I forget what Uber's product is called, but Uber Direct I think it's called, where you have something that needs to go point to point in a city. That was a flop from the beginning because the truth is is how consumers don't really have this need, business sort of have this need, and in 2014 when we were doing this, no one had this need. But we tried 15 versions of all these things before we eventually just said, "Okay, the food delivery thing is just popping off on all signals and we can make the unit economics work. People seem to want it. It's a super cool problem because we can enable independent restaurants with all these tools and allow them to compete with the big guys. We can take the real estate out of the equation. So you can have a real estate location that's non-prime, but if you have prime food, then you get to compete." So we're like, "Oh, this is a very interesting problem and we can really help local economies."
turns.zh: 就解决这些问题而言，我绝对不是房间里最聪明的人。所以，我会尽可能长时间地保持对各种想法的开放心态，直到一切开始融合起来。我认为，有很多理由需要对那些一开始看似糟糕的想法保持开放的心态——你只要继续深挖，就能判断自己是对是错。就拿这点来说，作为一个基本的哲学原则，我先从这里入手。当时我们做了一些疯狂的尝试。有一天，我在旧金山漫步，沿着市场街望去，那里有一家CVS、一家7-Eleven、一家CVS、一家Walgreens，还有一家7-Eleven。我就想：“这些便利店里能有多少种人们真正想要的商品呢？你为什么不把这些商品装进货车里，按个按钮，货车就来了，人们就能买到他们需要的便利商品——毕竟这些都是便利商品，何必为此烦恼呢？”（00:54:14）我们在华盛顿特区推出了这个项目，投入了10辆卡车，上面装了250种商品。但反响冷淡得令人发指。根本没人下单。我们意识到，我们对便利店的理解太肤浅了。当时的便利店就是：如果你没有香烟、啤酒、思乐冰等商品，就没人光顾。因此，我们对零售业一无所知，完全是个门外汉。这就是其中一个失败的例子。我们也研究过生鲜配送，但说实话，单位经济效益实在太差了，仓储物流等问题简直让人头疼。我认为Instacart在优化单位经济效益方面做得非常出色，而这恰恰是零售业最难攻克的难题。（00:54:56）我们尝试了多种配送模式，比如点对点配送。现在Uber的某个产品叫Uber Direct，专门解决城市内点对点配送的问题。但这个项目从一开始就注定失败，因为消费者根本没有这方面的需求，商家倒是有需求。但2014年我们做这个项目时，根本没人有这种需求。在尝试了15个版本后，我们最终认定：食品配送业务正如火如荼，我们能让单位经济效益达标，用户需求旺盛。这是一个很酷的商业模式，我们能用各种工具赋能独立餐厅，让它们与大平台竞争，还能省去实体店铺成本。即便选址不佳，只要食品质量过硬，就能参与竞争。所以我们觉得：“哦，这真是个很有趣的商业模式，能真正助力本地经济。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this ended up being, if I remember correctly, this basically saved Uber during COVID. Lyft didn't have something like this. And how big is this business at this point? Anything you share about just how important this turned out to be for Uber?
turns.zh: 如果我没记错的话，这项业务最终在新冠疫情期间拯救了Uber。Lyft没有类似的业务。那么这个业务现在规模有多大呢？能否分享一下它对Uber的重要性？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Yeah, of course. Well, we launched it in December of 2015 in Toronto and within two hours we had done $20,000 for the sales. It was crazy how quickly we saw that it was the right idea and the unit economics were good. And then, four and a half years later, I was at Uber for about six years, but it took us about a year and a half to figure this out. Four and a half years later, it was about $20 billion. So it was 0 to 20 billion in four and a half years, which is pretty good. Uber was very good at scaling things, but competitive market. Others did well. We beat a lot of people. Some people beat us. And then, now I think it's pushing 80 billion, and that's been for another four and a half years since I left. I think COVID turned it from 20, I left right before COVID, total coincidence, 20 to 50 in a year. So I mean, ride-sharing went this and food delivery just went to Pluto.
turns.zh: 是啊，当然。嗯，我们2015年12月在多伦多推出这项服务，两个小时内就实现了2万美元的销售额。当时我们很快意识到这是一个正确的决策，单位经济效益也很不错。四年半之后，我在Uber工作了大约六年，但我们花了大约一年半的时间才搞清楚这一点。四年半后，Uber的估值达到了约200亿美元。所以在四年半的时间里，估值从0增长到200亿，相当不错。Uber在扩展业务方面做得很出色，但市场竞争激烈。其他公司表现也不错。我们击败了许多竞争对手，也被一些对手超越。现在我认为Uber的估值已经接近800亿，而这距离我离开又过去了四年半。我觉得新冠疫情让估值从200亿飙升到500亿，而我离开前夕新冠疫情刚爆发，这纯属巧合。总之，网约车行业一度风生水起，而外卖业务却一蹶不振。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What luck. Well done.
turns.zh: 真是幸运啊。干得好。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Luck is part of the game. That's the other thing that's important to realize. Luck is part of the game, so do not begrudge people for luck. This industry is hard. All these things we're doing are really, really hard. Luck is just part of the game.
turns.zh: 运气也是成功的一部分。这是另一个需要认识到的重要点。运气是成功的一部分，所以不要嫉妒别人的好运。这行业太难了。我们所做的一切都非常、非常困难。运气只是成功的一部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe speaking that maybe not. One of your colleagues, Stephen Chau, who I am an investor in his new company, he worked with you at Uber Eats for a long time. He told me to ask you about the McDonald's story. I imagine that was just a big milestone, a big moment enough for you guys. So why'd you decide put McDonald's in Uber Eats and there's apparently a story of how you won that deal.
turns.zh: 也许你提到了也可能没有提到。你的同事之一，周世忠（Stephen Chau），我是他新公司的投资者，他在Uber Eats和你共事了很久。他让我问你关于麦当劳的故事。我想那对你们来说是一个重大的里程碑和转折点。那么，你们为什么决定把麦当劳引入Uber Eats呢？据说还有一个你们如何赢得这笔合作的故事。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: So it was interesting, and this just goes to maybe where sometimes ignorance leads you to accidentally the right answer. So we had launched Uber Eats and Uber had a global footprint and we were the only food delivery network with a global footprint excluding China. Everything at Uber needed to be launched globally. That was a very big part of the culture, et cetera, which is a lot of work and you can spread yourself too thin and cause other problems. But in this way it was good. My vision was, okay, let's help the little guy compete with all these chains. They have these systematized food systems and food is what makes a city amazing. And no one talks about the chain restaurant that they visited in Paris. They talk about the local place that they found and let's be part of that. That's who we want to be. (00:58:17): And so, McDonald's actually approached us and they said, "Hey, we'd love to do food delivery with you." And I said, "No." And they're like, "Hold on a second. We have 80 million consumers a day. You don't want to do this together?" I'm like, "It's not really our vibe right now." And so, I pushed them off for four or five months until my team is like, "You're insane. These people are going to put marketing behind it. They really want to do this. They want to lean in." So we actually had, because of that, I think it's hard to correlate these things, we ended up with this exclusive relationship with them, got an insane number of customers of... Chains at this point actually weren't really on food delivery networks because everybody was so worried about the unit economics, because they're so sensitive to the basket size. (00:59:00): And my approach was like, eh, figure it out, which is a very Uber culture thing. Okay, the basket's $17, it's our job to make that work, reduce the radius on the delivery, figure out the economics, maybe mark up some of the food someplace. There's always a way to figure it out. So we did it and then three months later the business just started hockey sticking again at a different level. And my team is just like, "Dude, you were so stubborn on this point," but I think it actually ended up being in net benefit because we got a great deal with them.
turns.zh: 嗯，这还挺有趣的，这或许说明有时候无知会让你意外地找到正确的答案。当时我们推出了Uber Eats，Uber在全球范围内都有业务，我们是除中国外唯一一家拥有全球配送网络的食品外卖平台。Uber的所有业务都需要在全球范围内同步推出，这在公司的文化中占据了重要地位，但这也意味着工作量巨大，而且容易分散精力导致其他问题。但从某种角度来看，这也不错。我的想法是，好吧，让小商家能与那些连锁店竞争。他们有系统化的食品供应体系，而美食才是让一座城市变得令人惊叹的元素。人们谈论的往往不是在巴黎去过的连锁餐厅，而是当地发现的美味店铺——我们就想成为这样的存在。（00:58:17）：后来麦当劳真的找到了我们，他们说：“嘿，我们想和你们合作外卖业务。”我说：“不行。”他们又说：“等等，我们每天有8000万消费者啊。你不想和我们合作吗？”我说：“现在这事儿不太合适。”于是我又拖了四五个月，直到我的团队说：“你疯了。这些人会全力投入的，他们真的很想做这事儿。”所以最终我们和他们达成了独家合作关系，获得了海量客户……当时连锁店根本没怎么加入外卖平台，因为大家都担心单位经济效益，对订单规模太敏感了。（00:59:00）：我的做法是，嗯，找到解决办法，这很符合Uber的文化。好吧，如果订单均价17美元，那我们就想办法降低配送半径，优化经济效益，或许在某些地方加价，总会有办法的。结果三个月后，业务量就暴增了。我的团队说：“老兄，你当时太固执了。”但我觉得最终还是有好处的，因为我们和他们达成了很棒的合作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the fact that you pushed him out helped you get a better deal is what I'm hearing. That's amazing.
turns.zh: 所以你推迟合作反倒帮了你们拿到了更好的协议，这才是关键。太棒了。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Yeah, I think that's the story he would be referencing. And then, the onboarding of it was crazy because we basically went global with them in six months, and at this point the business was less than two years old. So activating this, I don't even know, an 80-year-old company that expects processes to be in place and we have two of our office managers in New York managing it. It's just mayhem.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得他说的就是这个故事。然后，接入他们的系统真是疯狂，因为我们在六个月内就和他们全球同步了，而当时业务开展还不到两年。激活这个系统，天知道有多难。我们要和纽约的两位办公室经理一起管理一家有80年历史、期待流程规范的公司。简直就是一团乱麻。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm still sad In-N-Out is still not on any of these apps.
turns.zh: 我还是很遗憾In-N-Out至今还没上任何外卖平台。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Yeah, me too.
turns.zh: 是啊，我也这么觉得。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I remember someone was hacking it. There's all these ways people found a way around and they're like, "No, no. Okay, you're Postmates. We know we're not going to give you any food."
turns.zh: 我记得当时有人黑过他们的系统。人们总能找到各种方法绕过规则，还会说：“不，不行，你们是Postmates，我们知道不会给你们任何食物的。”

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Yes, love In-N-Out.
turns.zh: 是啊，我超爱In-N-Out的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You've touched on this idea of gross margins and margins, how obsessed you are with this. I wanted to spend a little time on here. I've heard just you're obsessed with understanding gross margins before going in on anything. Most founders have no idea what they're doing here. What have you learned about just what people should be paying attention to, what they might be forgetting when they think about just the feasibility of a business?
turns.zh: 您提到了毛利率和利润率的概念，看得出您对此十分着迷。我想在这里多谈谈这个话题。我听说您在投资项目前总会先深入研究毛利率。大多数创业者对此一知半解，根本不清楚如何理解毛利率的含义。您对创业者在评估商业可行性时容易忽视的关键点有何见解？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Yeah, look, it's one filter like many filters. There are certainly businesses that have low gross margins that are great businesses. Costco, Walmart, et cetera. Amazon talks about this all the time of there's companies that increase prices and there's companies at lower prices. But I would say that by and large, high gross margins combined with healthy churn curves are a very healthy sign for the business. I mean, think about it. If I were to sell you something and I can't mark it up a lot, how much value am I adding beyond what's in my hand? And if I'm not adding that much value, then what am I in the business of doing? And I'm in business of adding value. And it's not quite that simple. This is just a litmus test of when someone comes to me and they go, especially in a new business, and we deal with this. I dealt with this at Uber, I've dealt with it everywhere. (01:01:26): Someone comes up with an idea and they go, "We can get into this business and I think we can charge this and it'll get us to a 40% gross margin." And then, my next question is start at a 60% gross margin. Why does that not work? And they go, "Oh, well, the customer..." And immediately, you short circuit to what the real problem is. Oh, the customer has an alternative. Oh, okay, well who's the alternative? Oh, it's some offshoring company. Well, what's their gross margin? Oh, we don't know. You go find out. It's like 20% and they've been around for a long time and they have scaled operations. And you're like, okay, so your gross margin is going to go from 40 to 20 quicker than you think, and you're going to be in a world of hurt unless you do something to differentiate. (01:02:06): So I take gross margin is just a very coarse instrument, not a perfect instrument to think about, am I adding enough value? Am I differentiated? It's not perfect, but it's a very quick short circuit filter to even to see if someone's pitching you an idea, have they thought through this dynamic? Because if the response is gross margin is super low right now, but here's the dynamic I'm going after. And then you're like, "Oh, okay." And sometimes it's like, we'll just make it up with volume and then the gross margin will go negative for a while and you're like, "Wait, this doesn't work."
turns.zh: 是的，毛利率只是众多衡量标准之一。有很多毛利率低但经营出色的企业，比如好市多、沃尔玛等。亚马逊常提到，有些公司通过涨价来提高利润，有些则通过降低价格来竞争。但总体而言，高毛利率搭配健康的客户流失率曲线，是企业健康发展的标志。试想一下，如果我要卖给你一件商品，却没法加太多价钱，那我提供的价值除了手头现有资源之外还有多少？如果价值增益不明显，那我们做生意的意义何在？而我的核心观点是，毛利率是筛选项目的关键指标。当有人向我提出新创意时，尤其是在新兴领域，我们会遇到这种情况。我在优步时就处理过类似问题。有人提案：“我们能切入这个市场，定价能达到40%的毛利率。”我接着会问：“那如果毛利率从60%降到40%呢？”对方回答：“客户……” 然后瞬间暴露出核心问题：客户有替代方案。接着追问：“那替代方案是谁？”“是某家离岸生产商。”“他们的毛利率多少？”“不知道。”于是你去调查，发现毛利率只有20%，而且他们已经运营多年，规模化运作了。这时你会意识到，毛利率从40%降到20%比想象中快得多，如果不提升差异化优势，公司必将陷入困境。（01:01:26）所以毛利率只是个粗略衡量标准，不能完全替代深度分析，但它能快速筛选出项目是否值得投入。若对方回答毛利率很低，但又声称要追逐某种商业模式，这时你得警惕了。（01:02:06）毛利率只是个快捷过滤器，能快速判断创始人是否深思熟虑过商业逻辑。若对方回应“现在毛利率低，但我们有增长动能”，你要追问：“那毛利率从40%降到20%需要多久？”对方可能答：“很快。”这时你会意识到，除非提升差异化，否则毛利率会加速下滑，最终陷入亏损困境。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what I love about this is just a lens into is my idea good enough if studying, can I keep a high gross margin? Is there a reason why people in this space haven't been able to have a higher margin?
turns.zh: 所以我喜欢用毛利率这个指标来审视创意是否可行——能否维持高毛利率？这个领域为何普遍难以实现高毛利率？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. And like I said, it's meant to disqualify just you're doing these large for larger companies and everybody has ideas. And so, it's a way to cut through. Do you understand the machine that is going to need to be in place in two or three years? You might have a 70% gross margin now because the next question is why can't someone else do this? And if you have an answer of like, "Well, they can now, but they can't in two years, if we run really fast." Okay, we might have something. If they can now and they will be able to in two years, you're going to have margin compression.
turns.zh: 是啊，没错。就像我说的，这就是为了排除那些只为大公司做事的人，因为每个人都有想法。所以，这是一种突围之道。你理解未来两三年内需要建立的机制吗？你现在可能有70%的毛利率，但下一个问题是，为什么别人做不到？如果你回答说"他们现在能做到，但两年后做不到，如果我们行动够快"，那或许还有机会。但如果他们现在能做到，两年后也能做到，那你的毛利率就会被压缩。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along these lines I was just listening to, I think it was the a16z podcast. Alex Rampell I think was sharing this story about Costco, how as you said, their strategy is actually to keep margins very, very low because all their revenue comes from their membership. So they have something like 50 million members paying 100 bucks a month and that's their entire business. And so, they don't plan and they don't want to make money off the products.
turns.zh: 我最近听过a16z播客，亚历克斯·兰佩尔分享了关于好市多（Costco）的故事。正如你所说，他们的策略实际上是保持极低的毛利率，因为所有收入都来自会员制。所以他们有大约5000万会员，每月支付100美元，这就是他们的全部业务。他们不打算也不想从产品中赚钱。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Yeah, that's right. I mean, they're playing a slightly different game, not an expert on Costco, have spent some time with the company, but they use price as a way to get to scale. And so, they're basically saying if we discount, same with Walmart, we will get so much volume that we will just take the air out of the room for all of our competition. And so, then the question of, okay, so if you have a low gross margin today, in two or three years, once you land one of these centers in a market, why won't your margins to get eroded? The answer is because we will have already absorbed all of the demand. You try to go to 8% versus 10% gross margin, which I roughly think is what their gross margin is. That's going to be a really hard business. If you already have a habit with a customer, they have already built their weekly trips around you, you already have relationships with suppliers, you already have general managers that know how to stock inventory, that's not a straightforward exercise. So they're first to scale and then good luck competing with them.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。他们的玩法略有不同，我对好市多不是专家，但我和他们交流过。他们的定价策略是通过降价实现规模扩张。基本上，他们认为如果我们降价，和沃尔玛一样，我们能获得足够大的销量，把竞争对手挤出市场。那么问题来了，如果你现在毛利率低，两三年后，当你在某个市场开设中心后，为什么你的毛利率不会被侵蚀？答案是我们已经吸收了所有需求。假设你把毛利率从10%降到8%（我粗略估计他们的毛利率在10%左右），那生意会很难做。如果你已经和客户建立了习惯，他们每周的购物行程都围绕你展开，你和供应商关系稳固，总经理知道如何备货，这可不是件容易的事。所以他们先实现规模扩张，再来竞争就难了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Just a couple more questions. One is there's this term that I've heard that you often say and believe in is this idea of not losing is a precursor to winning.
turns.zh: 好的。再问几个问题。有个术语我常听到，你也认同，那就是“不输就是赢的先决条件”。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Yes, yes.
turns.zh: 是的，是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Talk about that.
turns.zh: 能讲讲这个吗？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Tech is a culture where portfolios are built by investors, and a lot of the narrative is controlled by investors frankly. Founders obviously participate, but this idea that you should just go for it is consensus. Just go for it. Who cares? Well, I don't know, if it's my life and I only have one moment to take a shot, I might want to just not just go for it. I might want to think for a little bit, and I think the best entrepreneurs, I have no data to back this up, but just these are my friend, this is my friend group. I think the best entrepreneurs and the best business owners look at the risk profile of the decisions that they're making and they try to make asymmetrically positive decisions all along the way. (01:05:51): And so, oftentimes I feel like we forget about the risk of a decision, and there's more to unpack there because I actually think taking highly risky decisions and then having it work out is a weird cultural thing too, because then how do you train people to do that? Because it's a very hard thing to take high risk decisions and be right enough because it creates a lot of volatility. But it goes back to my comment about the most important thing in founders, which is just this ability to persevere through. Survival is just part of the game, and most people just give up before they get their timing right, before they get the right insight with the customer before they get the right product in the market. And life can change quickly in tech. You can go from being a dog to being a hero in a very short period of time, but you're on this very, very long journey, but you have to survive for that condition to be met. (01:06:38): And so, then the question is is when you're in a hype cycle, I would argue that we are right now, everyone wants to go for it and then go for it more and then go for it more and go for it more and you don't realize, guys, all of our customers are going to be around in five years. They just want us to solve their problems. We have to be around to solve their problem for them. And so, survival is a precursor to that. So let's not put ourselves in position that could potentially compromise the enterprise along the way. It doesn't mean don't take risks, but think about how you calculate it.
turns.zh:
科技行业的文化是，由投资者构建投资组合，而行业叙事在很大程度上由投资者主导。创始人显然会参与其中，但"放手去做"的共识却盛行。"放手去做吧！谁在乎呢？"但说实话，如果这是我的人生，且只有一次出手的机会，我或许不会只顾一味冲动。或许我会多思考片刻。我认为最优秀的创业者——虽然我没有数据支持，但就我身边朋友而言——他们会审视所做决策的风险曲线，并始终致力于做出不对称正向的决策。（01:05:51）：所以我常觉得，我们常常忽视决策的风险。这里有更多值得深思之处，因为我认为冒高风险决策并最终成功，本身就是一种文化现象。毕竟如何培养人们做出这种决策的能力呢？冒高风险决策并最终成功，固然令人钦佩，但这也伴随着巨大波动。但这又回到了我关于创业者最重要品质的观点——就是坚持不懈的能力。生存是游戏的一部分，大多数人在把握时机、洞察客户需求、将产品推向市场之前就选择放弃了。科技行业的变化速度极快。你可能在短时间内从籍籍无名一跃成为英雄，但这条路漫长而曲折，而生存是达成目标的前提。
（01:06:38）：所以问题在于，当我们身处炒作周期时——比如我们当下所处的阶段——每个人都想冲冲冲、再冲冲冲、再冲冲冲，却忽视了一个关键：五年后我们的客户仍会存在。他们只希望我们解决他们的问题。而我们必须持续为此奋斗。生存是成功的先决条件。所以别把自己置于可能危及企业存续的境地。这并不意味着不要冒险，而是要理性评估风险。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love how clear it is that this lesson and many of the lessons along these lines have come from just failure and things not working out and things breaking, which is the best outcome.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏这一点：这堂课以及诸多类似的教训，往往源于失败、项目夭折和系统崩盘——而这些恰恰是最宝贵的经验。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: If you ever get on the other side of a high reward, high risk decision, it is so painful because you are just cooked. You are done, and often there's no way out.
turns.zh: 如果你曾在高回报高风险决策中幸存下来，那种痛苦感会刻骨铭心。你彻底失败了，且往往无路可退。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a story along those lines that comes to mind or an example of that?
turns.zh: 你能想到类似的案例或故事吗？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Well, this is where it is together on why I try to be so I think you can spend a little bit of time thinking upfront to save yourself a lot of pain downstream. I had this business not worth detailing it, but after the bubble burst in 2001, I'm like, "I'm going to self-fund a business. I'm going to build a profitable business. I want to prove that I can do this." And we had started Scour, which had all the things we talked about. And so, what I did is I'm like, I was a golfer and frankly, there was nothing to do in tech. (01:08:03): So I started selling golf clubs on the internet and I was making real money and I might've learned more from this business than any other because I started on eBay and I was 22, and I didn't really understand that my margins would come down because anyone can do this, but I was one of the first ones to do it, so I was making a ton of money and then I built this business and then I just failed to recognize I had a lot of hubris. I was like, "Oh, if I could just buy all the used golf clubs in America, I can be the market maker for prices," and don't people do that?
turns.zh: 嗯，这就是我为何努力做到这一点的原因。我觉得你可以提前花点时间思考，省去日后很多痛苦。我曾有过一段不值一提的创业经历，但2001年泡沫破裂后，我决定自筹资金创办一家盈利性企业，证明自己的能力。于是我们创办了Scour公司，具备了我们此前提到的所有要素。当时我还是个高尔夫球爱好者，坦白说，科技领域没什么可做的。（01:08:03）于是我开始在网上卖高尔夫球杆，确实赚了不少钱。通过这段经历，我学到的东西比其他任何业务都多——我22岁时在eBay上创业，对利润率可能下降的风险毫无准备，但作为最早入局者，我确实赚了大钱。后来我把公司做大了，却没能意识到自己的自大心理。我曾想：“如果我能收购全美所有二手高尔夫球杆，就能成为价格操盘手。”可别人不是早就这么做了吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this ambition. That's great.
turns.zh: 我欣赏你的这种雄心壮志，太棒了。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: And it's just like it's madness to actually think about the practicality of that. And so, I just didn't spend the time thinking and then I ended up in this business. The business was profitable, it got to a couple million of revenue, whatever, paid me a dividend for a while, but it was painful the entire way.
turns.zh: 但现实中去考虑这种想法简直是疯狂。结果我没花时间思考，最终把公司搞砸了。公司确实盈利过，有段时间营收达几百万美元，还分过红，但整个过程充满痛苦。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love the spectrum of experiences you've had. You've sold golf clubs, you're helping achieve AGI, you could say. There's also a whole part of your career. We haven't talked about where you built tasers and body cams and drones and all these things. Also, peer-to-peer file sharing before anyone else. Final topic I just want to spend a little time on based on this experience is hiring and building teams, something that I know you have a really strong take on. That I've been hearing a lot on this podcast recently is this idea of it's more important to build the right team than find the most optimal top talent. Talk about that, why that's so interesting and important.
turns.zh: 你的人生经历真是丰富多彩。卖过高尔夫球杆，现在又在助力实现通用人工智能（AGI）。还有你职业生涯的其他部分，比如研发泰瑟枪、随身摄像头、无人机等产品。更早之前还搞过点对点文件共享。基于这些经历，我想重点探讨一下招聘和团队建设。你在这方面有很深刻的见解。最近在播客上听到很多观点：组建合适的团队比寻找最顶尖人才更重要。你能谈谈这其中的逻辑和重要性吗？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: As of late, I've developed a more nuanced view of this, which is for certain roles, you absolutely need the right experience in this current market. You see this with researchers, because the market's moving so fast, you don't have time to train up some people, so you actually have to go find people either who have the right relationships with customers that you want to get or you have to, who might not check other boxes but are awesome at that, might not check the classic boxes that I think you're referencing of they're a problem solver, they can grow with the company, they have a high trajectory, et cetera. I would say that's 5% of the roles in the company, but very important whenever speed to market is important. (01:10:09): And then, for interviewing, I just interview for three things and I have to interview across all kinds of expertises, which is hard. I can't be an expert in everything. And so, I reduce it down to just three things, which is like, are you a curious problem solver and can you articulate that verbally? Can you work across people? Are you humble enough to work across and are you a good leader? And if you just do those three things, I think you have a pretty high chance of success, at least in an organization that I'm running, because the world's changing. So you do need people that are adaptable. So all the experience is not necessarily one-to-one relevant. (01:10:53): And then, the working across to your team point, this actually came up at Uber Eats. So when I was building the Uber Eats management team, I'm not sure if this was mentioned to you from that group, but whenever I would hire people, I was trying to compose almost like an organism of strengths and then minimize the conflicts. That management team for the most part outside of some of the operations side, but for the most part, that management team was the same management team from day one when we had nothing to $20 billion. And I just believed that the team, knowing each other's strengths and weaknesses and being able to compensate for each other was more important than the classic advice you get around, "Well, that person hasn't seen this much scale." And you're like, "Well, yeah, but can they learn it?" I learned it. So you do have to kind of believe in people a little bit, which is my job, not necessarily their job. And so, I mean, these are people systems. They're not straightforward rules-based things you can apply.
turns.zh:
最近，我对此有了更深刻的认识：在当前的市场环境下，某些职位确实需要具备恰当的经验。这在研究人员身上体现得尤为明显，因为市场变化太快，你没有时间去培养新人——你必须要么找到与目标客户关系紧密的人才，要么找到虽不完全符合传统标准但在某个领域极为出色的人才。比如，他们或许不符合你所提及的典型标准——比如他们是问题解决者，能随公司一起成长，具有高潜力等。我认为这类人才在公司中只占5%，但在追求快速上市的环境下至关重要。

（01:10:09）接下来是面试环节。我只关注三个核心要点，而且需要跨领域面试不同专业人才，这实在不易。我无法面面俱到，所以把重点缩减至三个问题：你是否有好奇心强的解决问题能力？能否清晰口头表达？能否跨团队协作？是否足够谦逊？能否成为优秀的领导者？只要做好这三点，在我管理的公司里成功几率极高，毕竟世界在变，我们需要适应力强的人才。并非所有经验都直接相关。

（01:10:53）再说团队协作这点，在Uber Eats时我就深有体会。在组建Uber Eats管理团队时，我不确定是否有人向你们提及过，但每次招聘时，我都试图构建一个优势互补的团队，尽量减少冲突。除了部分运营岗位外，这个管理团队从初创到市值200亿美元始终保持一致。我坚信，团队成员了解彼此的优势与不足，并能相互弥补，这比“此人缺乏大规模经验”之类的传统标准更重要。毕竟，经验可以后天培养——我自己就是个例子。所以你得相信员工的潜力，这既是我的职责，也是他们的自我修养。因此，这些人才选拔机制并非一刀切的规则，而是需要因人而异的灵活性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I especially love this advice because there's all this talk about what skills will matter in this world of AI doing all our jobs, and it feels like these three buckets are maybe the same thing, just are they good at solving problems? Are they good leaders? Can they collaborate well with other people?
turns.zh: 我尤其喜欢这种观点。当人们热议AI将取代人类所有工作的未来时，或许这三个核心要素其实是一回事：解决问题的能力、领导才能、团队协作能力。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Yeah, I don't think that the core rise of humanity, it will change, and I think that these things are pretty core to how humans have been successful for a long time.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为人类的核心优势不会改变。这些特质长期以来一直是人类成功的基石。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of that, I'm going to take us to a recurring segment of this podcast that I call AI Corner, where I ask folks this question, what's some way that you've found a use for AI in your day-to-day life in your work that makes you more effective, get more done, get better stuff done?
turns.zh: 说到这，我要引出本期播客的固定环节——“AI角落”。在这一环节，我会向嘉宾提问：在日常工作中，你如何利用AI提升效率、产出更优质成果？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Honestly, when I came into Scale, so my history was in consumer and I've done some application level stuff with government, and this space is moving so quickly. AI is my, I use it as a tutor. As these new concepts come up, I have a lot of people in the company who can educate me on the nuances of the technicals of all of, excuse me, the technical nature of the data and the products, but they only have so much time. And honestly, there's new concepts coming up all the time and I need to stay on top of it. (01:13:01): So it might sound crazy, but a large percentage of my job is not dealing with the engineering issues related to AI. I'm managing an organization, but I love understanding it. It's one of the most enjoyable, rewarding parts of my job is to learn from all these AI researchers, but they don't always have the time to do it, so I use it as a tutor. I turn on voice mode and talk to it on my way into work. So I think that's probably the most impactful thing that I use it for that's also relevant to this topic.
turns.zh: 老实说，我加入Scale时，之前一直专注于消费者领域，也做过一些政府应用层面的项目。但这个领域发展太快了。人工智能对我来说，就像个导师。随着新概念不断涌现，公司里有很多同事能给我讲解技术细节的细微之处——比如数据和产品的技术性问题，但他们毕竟时间有限。说实话，新概念层出不穷，我必须紧跟潮流。（01:13:01）：这听起来可能有点疯狂，但我工作的很大一部分并非处理与人工智能相关的工程问题。我负责管理团队，但我热爱钻研这门技术。学习人工智能研究者的知识，是我工作中最有趣、最有收获的部分。不过他们并非总有时间授课，所以我就把它当作导师。我上班路上会开启语音模式，与它交流。我觉得这可能是最有效的应用场景，也是与本话题最相关的部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I do exactly the same thing, especially when I'm prepping for this podcast. What exactly is this? I think about when you say this, I did an interview with the founders of Perplexity a few years ago asking about how they work at Perplexity, and the founders said that before, they were ruled, before they ask a question of anyone on the team, they have to ask AI first. And I was just like, "That's crazy." Now, it's so obvious. But back then, I was like, "That's an insane way of working. I've never heard of this before." Just a sign of how ahead of the curve they were.
turns.zh: 我也经常这么做，尤其是为这期播客做准备时。具体来说，我几年前采访了Perplexity的创始人，询问他们的工作方式。他们说，在向团队成员提问前，必须先向AI咨询。我当时就觉得：“这太疯狂了。”现在看来，这再正常不过了。但当时我觉得：“这工作方式太离谱了。我从未听过这种操作。” 这恰恰说明他们超前于时代。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Yeah, I think number two would be I'll take internal documents and I'll ask, what's the most important thing in this document? And I'm shocked, and then I'll read it and just double check, but I'm shocked at how good it is at just pulling out. There's so much in organizations that is like, I don't know what you want me to say and I don't know what I need to know, but we each have our own agendas, and so this matching of, and so then there's this huge broadcast problem where it's like, of all of the information you might want to receive, what's actually important to you? And so, I use it a lot for that too.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为第二个用途是，我会拿起内部文件，问：“这份文件最重要的内容是什么？” 结果总是让我震惊。然后再通读一遍，我会惊讶于它能如此精准地提取信息。组织中有很多信息，比如“我不知道你想让我说什么，也不知道我需要知道什么”，每个人都有自己的议程。因此，存在巨大的信息过载问题——面对海量信息，哪些才是真正重要的？所以我也经常用它来解决这个问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. That's a really good tip. I use it for legal documents, just like what do they know about what they're trying to do here for me or against me? Jason, is there anything else you wanted to share or leave listeners with, maybe double down on a point before we get to a very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 太棒了。这真是个好建议。我用它处理法律文件，比如他们对我的案子了解多少？杰森，你还有什么想和听众分享的吗？或者在进入激动人心的闪电问答环节前，再强调一下重点？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. I mean, I think the really important, the reason why I'm doing this, the reason why want to spend time here outside of wanting to be on the show for a while and being a long-term listener is, our long-time listener, excuse me, is there's a lot of amazing work going on at Scale. The teams are working super hard, we're delivering a ton of value for our customers. The public narrative has not represented the work that the people here are doing and the work that our customers are doing with what we're doing for them. And I just think that deserves the respect and reward that all those people are putting in, and we'd like people to know that.
turns.zh: 当然。我觉得我做这件事的真正意义所在——除了想参加节目、长期收听之外——在于我们在Scale做了很多了不起的工作。团队成员非常努力，为客户创造了巨大价值。但公众对我们的工作的认知与实际成果存在巨大落差。我认为这些人付出的努力和取得的成果都值得尊重和认可，我们希望人们能了解这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I appreciate you saying all that. With that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. We've got five questions for you. You ready?
turns.zh: 非常感谢你分享这些观点。现在，我们要进入激动人心的闪电问答环节了。我们有五个问题等着你回答。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Yeah, let's go for it.
turns.zh: 好的，开始吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you find yourself recommending most to other people?
turns.zh: 你最常向他人推荐的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Some of this is going to sound interesting. The Selfish Gene is one of my favorite books.
turns.zh: 接下来有些问题可能听起来挺有趣的。《自私的基因》是我最喜欢的书之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Love that book. I don't know if anyone's ever mentioned, it was one of the most influential books for me too. So sorry, keep going.
turns.zh: 我超爱这本书。不知道有没有人提过，它对我影响最大。抱歉，继续。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Yes. I think Selfish Gene. Road Less Traveled, I've read more than once. I mean, it's just one of the classic human psychology book. And then, I think in business, I think Good to Great. It's not the read that you're going to be most excited to enjoy on a vacation, but it's pretty much right, and I think we should take advice from people who have analyzed these business problems before because not a lot's changed, but we keep acting like everything's changed.
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得《自私的基因》很棒。《少有人走的路》我读过不止一遍。这本书堪称人类心理学的经典之作。在商业领域，我推荐《从优秀到卓越》。这本书不一定是度假时最爱读的书，但确实很实用。我认为我们应该借鉴那些分析过商业难题的人的建议，毕竟很多问题本质上并未发生变化，但我们却总觉得一切都变了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's crazy about that book, you look at all the companies they talk about, I haven't read in a while, but just the whole book is about companies that last, I believe, or maybe that's the other book, I don't know. But anyway, all the companies that they talk about, I don't know if they're still around. It's so hard for a business to last a long, long time.
turns.zh: 这本书最有趣的地方在于，书中提到的那些公司，我有些已经好久没听说过了。整本书讲的都是经久不衰的公司，我记得还有另一本书讲这个主题，但具体哪本我记不清了。总之，书中提到的那些公司，不知道现在是否还存在。让一家企业长久存续实在太难了。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: I would also recommend Thinking Slow and Fast, that's the... Yes.
turns.zh: 我还推荐《思考，快与慢》，这本书……对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thinking, Fast and Slow.
turns.zh: 《思考，快与慢》。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Thinking, Fast and Slow. Excuse me, sorry. It's been like a decade since I read it, but just in terms of point there being human biases are very important to understand.
turns.zh: 《思考，快与慢》。抱歉，我有十年没读这本书了，但书中关于人类偏见的论述确实很重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's really crazy to me about that book and Kahneman in general, someone asked them just, how's your life been impacted by learning all these biases humans have? He's like, "Not much. I have the same biases. Knowing them doesn't really help me avoid them."
turns.zh: 对我来说，关于这本书和卡尼曼的观点最有趣的是，有人问他：学习这些人类偏见后，生活有何改变？他回答：“没太大变化。我自己也有这些偏见。了解它们并不能帮我避免它们。”

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: See, I find myself checking myself. Whenever I get super convicted on something now I will be like, okay, what is the list of things that I'm inclined to do to try to catch myself? Because I think we're most inclined to have these bad decisions impulsively, which is what I think the book is largely about. I mean, it's a long book.
turns.zh: 所以我现在会经常自我审视。每当我对某件事深信不疑时，就会反思：我可能会采取哪些措施来提醒自己？因为我觉得我们最容易在冲动下做出错误决策，这正是这本书的主旨所在。说真的，这本书太长了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So long. Oh, my God. It feels like that's where AI can help us in the future. Just like, "Hey, Jason, are you sure this isn't framing a fact or whatever?"
turns.zh: 太长了。天哪。这感觉正是人工智能未来能帮到我们的地方。比如，“嘿，杰森，你确定这不是在曲解事实之类的？”

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Next question. Do you have a favorite recent movie or TV show that you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 好的。下一个问题。你最近有没有特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Most of the movies I watch are with my kids, so I wish I had something deep and profound.
turns.zh: 我看的大多数电影都是和孩子们一起看的，所以我希望能推荐一些有深度有内涵的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, kids content also is a very acceptable-
turns.zh: 不，儿童内容也完全可以接受——

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: The Formula 1 movie I thought was really good. I mean, it's a classic action movie. I don't think it informs anything in AI or business, but it's good to check out from the craziness of tech once in a while.
turns.zh: 《F1赛车手》这部电影我觉得很棒。经典动作片。虽然它和AI或商业没太大关联，但偶尔从科技的疯狂中抽身出来看看还是不错的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a product you recently discovered that you really love? Could be an app, could be clothing, could be a kitchen gadget, anything along those lines?
turns.zh: 最近有没有发现什么特别喜欢的产品？可能是某款应用、衣物，或者厨房小工具之类的。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: VO3. Not totally new, but when I was in high school, I wanted to be a screenwriter. I actually grew up in the Bay Area and everybody was an engineer, but I wanted be a screenwriter. And so, I went back and I got the first page of one of my old scripts, which not good scripts, but I got the first page. I took a picture of the script and I fed it to VO3, and I said, "Make this scene," and it got it right.
turns.zh: VO3。其实不算全新，但我高中时就想成为编剧。我在湾区长大，那里的人大多是工程师，但我执意想当编剧。后来我找出了一份旧剧本的第一页，虽然不算特别出色，但总归是第一页。我把剧本拍了照，输入到VO3里，然后说：“把这场戏拍出来。”结果它拍得特别准确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: I was shocked. I was just absolutely shocked that you could just take a picture of a script. And so, now I'm thinking about that for how do I use these tools for family videos? Some of the grad tools now with making live images more active, I think are really interesting. I think they need one more step of iteration, but I think those are going to be really emotionally life-changing for people because just a little bit of movement in an image from a grandparent or a relative or whatever you haven't seen in a while, it really does make a big emotional impact on you.
turns.zh: 我太震惊了。就觉得你只要拍张剧本照片就能让AI理解，这简直不可思议。现在我在想，如何把这些工具应用到家庭影像中？现在一些图像活力增强的工具真的很有趣。我觉得它们还需要进一步优化，但这些功能真的能给人们带来情感上的变革。比如，祖父母或亲戚的旧影像只要有一点动态，都会给人带来强烈的情感冲击。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that when you play with these tools, you probably can think about, oh, here's the people that help train this thing. Here's the people that helped on the problem that it had.
turns.zh: 玩这些工具时，你可能会想到，哦，这些人参与了模型训练，帮助解决了问题。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: I was actually talking to someone who was working on VO3, and I told him the script thing and he goes, "Oh, actually scripts. Yeah, no, the way the data is formatted in a script, that would actually be very good." Because they start with set looks dark interior, this character says it in this raspy voice, and so it gives you all the instructions in the script.
turns.zh: 我之前和做VO3的人聊起剧本的事，他说："哦，剧本的数据格式确实很适合训练。"因为剧本通常开头是"场景设定：昏暗的室内"，角色用沙哑的声音说话，所有指令都清晰明了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, man, just unlocked a whole new business unit right there. Two more questions. One is do you have a favorite life motto that you often think about, find useful in work or in life?
turns.zh: 天哪，我刚刚开拓了一个全新的业务领域。再问两个问题：有没有你常挂在嘴边、觉得对工作或生活很有用的座右铭？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Yeah. The end is never the end. That's my favorite internal saying, and it goes to the comments before about survival being a precursor, surviving being a precursor to thriving. You got to survive before you thrive, which is your brain tells you, and along these entrepreneurial journeys, I think this is most applicable. I mean, this is the hardest journey anyone can go on. If you go on this journey for five years, you are mentally harder than 99.9% of the population. People don't understand the Chinese water torture of having self-doubt and having things go wrong, et cetera. (01:20:31): And so, more tactically, you get this when you're working out like in a day like, "Oh, I'm too tired. I need to stop." But the truth is is you can keep going and the world's going to keep spinning. So I find in the moments where it's just the hardest or you have this hard decision that seems impassable and your body, you're having this visceral reaction to this is impassable, just to remind yourself that I'm going to wake up tomorrow. This isn't the end. There's another end somewhere. I just find that to unlock me to be like, okay, there might not be a perfect solution, there might be an imperfect solution, but it's a solution so let's just keep going.
turns.zh: 有。"终点永远不是终点。"这是我最常用的内心箴言。它呼应了之前关于生存是成功的前提，繁荣是生存的延续的观点。你必须先生存下来，才能繁荣。这是大脑告诉你的，在创业之路上，最适用不过了。毕竟这是最艰难的旅程。坚持五年，你的心智强度就超过99.9%的人。人们不理解自我怀疑、事与愿违等心理折磨。（01:20:31）：从更实际的角度讲，比如锻炼时想"太累了，停下吧"。但事实上，只要继续前进，世界就会继续运转。在最艰难的时刻，或是面对看似不可逾越的决策时，身体的本能反应会告诉你"这不可逾越"。这时你要提醒自己：明天太阳还会升起。这不是终点，终点在别处。我发现这样能帮我解锁心智：或许没有完美解决方案，但总有不完美的办法，那就继续吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question. You helped create Uber Eats. I imagine you're still a power user of Uber Eats. You have a favorite restaurant on Uber Eats that maybe people should know about, maybe that you order most from?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。你参与创建了Uber Eats。我想你现在仍然是Uber Eats的重度用户。你在Uber Eats上有没有特别喜欢的餐厅，或许值得推荐给大家？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: I order a shocking amount of McDonald's actually. Despite my original story, it's the family treat in the house. I would say that that's probably the top thing that we order.
turns.zh: 说实话，我点麦当劳的次数多得惊人。尽管我最初不太喜欢与全球连锁品牌合作，但偶尔享用一下也不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, man, I'm worried for your health, but I love, I haven't had McDonald's so long. This is like, maybe I should give it another-
turns.zh: 天哪，我真替你的健康担忧，不过我也很久没吃麦当劳了。或许我该再试试——

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: I mean, more practically we will order mixed greens or tender greens or something like that on a day-to-day basis, but I think that the more notable, surprising thing is is that despite my initial aversion to working with a global chain, it's a good treat once in a while. You just shouldn't have it all the time.
turns.zh: 更实际点说，我们日常会点混合蔬菜沙拉或嫩叶蔬菜之类的，但最值得一提的是，尽管我最初对与全球连锁品牌合作心存顾虑，但偶尔享受一下也不错。关键是别老吃这些。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Jason, this was incredible. I really appreciate you making time for this. I'm really honored to be the first chat you've had since taking over at Scale. Where can folks find you online if they want to maybe reach out, learn more about what you're, I don't know, maybe join Scale. Where do you want to point people to and how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 杰森，这次交流太棒了。感谢你抽出时间接受采访。很荣幸能成为你接管Scale后首位受访嘉宾。如果大家想了解更多信息、加入Scale，或者想联系你，应该去哪里呢？

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. I'm @jdroege, J-D-R-O-E-G-E on X. That's probably the easiest way to follow me, keep up with things and you can shoot me a DM if you like. And so, I think that's how you would keep in touch and, sorry, what was your other question? Sorry.
turns.zh: 当然可以。我在X上叫@jdroege，J-D-R-O-E-G-E。这是关注我的最便捷方式。大家可以给我发私信交流。另外，我觉得保持联系的最佳方式是——对了，你的另一个问题是什么？抱歉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you're hiring, I don't know, where should people go check it out if you are, and then also just-
turns.zh: 如果你们正在招聘，我想知道如果有职位空缺，人们该去哪里查看？然后——

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Absolutely. Just go to scale.com, go to our careers page, and we have 250 open roles. To the point about we're in business and we're growing, we're hiring a ton of people. Our data business is growing, our applications and services business is growing like crazy, and so we're going to need a lot of people to help us on that journey.
turns.zh: 当然可以。直接访问scale.com，进入我们的招聘页面，目前有250个职位空缺。说到业务扩展和增长，我们正在招聘大量人才。我们的数据业务正在蓬勃发展，应用和服务业务也增长迅速，所以我们需要大量人才助力发展。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You guys just signed some insanely large contracts with the government I was reading.
turns.zh: 我看到你们刚和政府签了两份数亿美元的合同。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Two $100 million contracts.
turns.zh: 两份各1亿美元的合同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: $100 million contracts.
turns.zh: 对，就是1亿美元。不是一份，而是两个月内签了两份。所以没错，我们的联邦政府业务进展顺利。企业业务也不错，国际政府业务同样蒸蒸日上，市场需求巨大。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: 100, yeah. We didn't sign just one. We signed two in one month, so yes, no, our federal business is doing well. Our enterprise business is doing well. Our international government's business is doing well. There's a lot of demand out there.
turns.zh: 有些销售人员拿到了丰厚的佣金。干得好。杰森，非常感谢你今天参与交流。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Some salespeople are getting some great commissions. Good job. Jason, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 是的，谢谢。很荣幸能来做客。很高兴能与大家交流，尤其是在我接管Scale的初期阶段。

turns.speaker: Jason Droege
turns.en: Yeah, thank you. Honor to be a guest here. Super excited to be with you, especially so early in the journey, or at least my journey here leading Scale.
turns.zh: 是的，谢谢。很荣幸能做客。特别开心能与你们交流，尤其是在我接管Scale的初期阶段。

turns.en: Appreciate it. Thanks for coming. Thanks for joining us. Bye, everyone. Thank you so much for listening.
